59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.title: The Supply-Side Effect of Immigration on Prices: Evidence from Nursing Homes
59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.author: Izabela Wnuk-Soares
59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.summary: We study how immigration affects prices through changes in labor supply. Using policy-driven increases in immigration to Germany and administrative data covering the universe of nursing homes, we find that one additional foreign-born woman per 100 residents reduces nursing-home care prices by 2.6 percent. The price effects are concentrated in more competitive markets. Examining potential mechanisms, we find that immigration lowers labor costs as nursing homes shift toward lower-paid foreign-born workers. We find no evidence of declines in inspection-based measures of quality or of scale effects. Finally, immigration increases the use of informal care, potentially strengthening competitive pressure from the broader care market.

59ec699e9f:1c8d3748e52f0cc5.title: AI-Augmented Capital-Skill Complementarity
59ec699e9f:1c8d3748e52f0cc5.author: Roberto Pinheiro
59ec699e9f:1c8d3748e52f0cc5.summary: We model artificial intelligence (AI) as a distinct capital input in a nested CES aggregate production function that extends work done by Krusell et al. (2000) and embed it in a dynamic general equilibrium economy. By bringing the model to the data, we estimate the degree to which AI either substitutes for or complements the other production inputs at the aggregate level. We find that AI is complementary to the high-skill–equipment composite and that the AI weight in production remains small. We then use the model to study how this complementarity shapes the macroeconomic and distributional effects of AI capital accumulation. The estimated model implies different effects of alternative AI shocks. A rise in the AI usage share is contractionary as it increases reliance on a scarce complementary input. A fall in AI prices is expansionary due to the lower cost of accumulating AI capital. A tax on AI capital income raises limited revenue while the AI capital stock remains small, but can finance welfare-improving transfers as the AI price falls. A large-scale universal basic income (UBI) funded jointly by a consumption tax slows AI investment with welfare gains for low-skill workers at the expense of losses for high-skill workers and entrepreneurs. On the measurement side, we construct a quality-adjusted AI price index from hedonic regressions and build a corresponding AI capital stock.

59ec699e9f:1f9e3fda07812288.title: Crime, Spatial Reallocation, and Employment Dynamics: Evidence on Firm-Size Heterogeneity from Mexico City
59ec699e9f:1f9e3fda07812288.author: Monserrat Zuñiga Loreto
59ec699e9f:1f9e3fda07812288.summary: This paper examines the relationship between neighborhood crime and firm employment in Mexico City. Using a balanced panel of 2, 354 Basic Geostatistical Areas (AGEBs) for 2017--2022, we estimate Spatial Durbin Models with AGEB fixed effects, lagged and winsorized crime variables, and differential trends by dominant firm-size stratum, decomposing total effects into direct and indirect components. At the aggregate level, robberies are negatively associated with employment in the AGEBs where they occur, alongside positive spillovers toward neighboring areas. This aggregate pattern conceals substantial heterogeneity: large firms (101 or more employees) are the only stratum with a negative and significant direct effect, whereas small firms (0--10 employees) show a positive direct effect, consistent with structural immobility and the local reallocation of displaced demand. Medium-sized firms show negative but imprecisely estimated effects. A dynamic specification preserves these signs but is weakly identified once persistence is absorbed. Crime appears to reallocate employment across the firm-size distribution and across space rather than uniformly contracting local labor demand.

59ec699e9f:30a9651e21805b4f.title: The Long-Term Effects of Labor Market Restrictions on Women’s Cognitive Aging
59ec699e9f:30a9651e21805b4f.author: Dorly Deegdijk
59ec699e9f:30a9651e21805b4f.summary: This study examines the causal effect of labor market restrictions faced by women in early adulthood on later-life cognitive functioning. To identify this effect, we exploit an exogenous policy change in the Netherlands that removed restrictions on married women's access to paid employment in 1957. Our study draws on data from the Longitudinal Aging Study Amsterdam, an ongoing cohort study of older individuals. We focus on individuals aged 75 and older born between 1928 and 1947. We first examine how work restrictions in early adulthood shape lifetime employment. Next, we assess how these work restrictions affect women’s later-life cognitive outcomes exploiting an exogenous change in labor restriction laws and complement this with an instrumental variables approach. The estimation results indicate that restricted access to paid employment for women in early adulthood reduced labor force participation and occupational prestige over the life course. These reduced labor market opportunities, in turn, led to poorer cognitive functioning after age 75. We also find some suggestive evidence that these restrictions resulted in faster cognitive decline. Taken together, our findings indicate that restrictions on women’s access to paid employment adversely affect cognitive functioning, thereby contributing to cognitive disparities between men and women in later life. More broadly, they highlight the long-term cognitive benefits of sustained labor market engagement and cognitively stimulating work, with potential implications for dementia prevention.

59ec699e9f:3bf831fa255a51f9.title: Matching and Mentoring: Effects of Managers on Worker Productivity
59ec699e9f:3bf831fa255a51f9.author: Chengyuan Hua
59ec699e9f:3bf831fa255a51f9.summary: This paper studies how managers matter for worker productivity by exploiting manager moves in Major League Baseball. I first show that manager effects are primarily match-specific using an AKM-type model. Then, staggered difference-in-differences results show positive effects of shared characteristics, including same position, both lefties, and same hometown. Effects of same position and both lefties are larger than same hometown. Effects are more pronounced for younger and less productive workers, indicating that mentoring is the primary mechanism while in-group bias is secondary. Finally, there is suggestive evidence that a managerâ€™s productivity as a worker is not a positive characteristic.

59ec699e9f:5f08d505bc269652.title: World War I and Female Labor Force Participation: The Case of England and Wales
59ec699e9f:5f08d505bc269652.author: Milner, Benjamin
59ec699e9f:5f08d505bc269652.summary: Combining district-level measures of World War I military fatalities with full-count census microdata, we show that wartime mortality increased postwar female labor force participation in England and Wales. Women shifted away from traditionally female occupations, while military deaths increased the shares of single and widowed women, whose participation rates were higher. Yet the overall effect of military mor-tality on postwar female labor force participation remained modest. A harmonized comparison with France suggests that stronger internal migration in England and Wales rapidly dissipated local marriage- and labor-market imbalances, while more generous pensions for war widows weakened their labor supply response.

59ec699e9f:c9bac5dd6367f0dd.title: Beyond the Paycheck: Using Fringe Benefits to Attract a Broader Pool of Applicants
59ec699e9f:c9bac5dd6367f0dd.author: Thea S. Zoellner
59ec699e9f:c9bac5dd6367f0dd.summary: Many firms in tight labor markets recruit for highly gender-segregated occupations, leaving them, in effect, drawing from only half the potential labor pool. We study how firms can use fringe benefits to attract workers and influence occupational choice. Unlike occupation-specific recruiting strategies, fringe benefits can be added to any occupation; they are also easily tailored, implemented, and scaled. Using a personalized and incentivized discrete choice experiment, we present participants with job options that match their skills and work task preferences. Within each option, we vary salary, occupation, and fringe benefits that adolescents had classified as gender-neutral, male-typed, or female-typed. We find that fringe benefits are highly valued: their effect is around a third as large as having prior interest in the occupation. Neutral and stereotypical benefits in particular improve perceptions of the firm across multiple dimensions. Furthermore, we find substantial gender differences. Female-typed benefits deter male participants, whereas all other benefit-participant combinations have a positive effect. Female participants value benefits more when those benefits are paired with an atypical occupation, and we find suggestive evidence that this reflects benefits alleviating concerns about limited support in such roles. In addition, male-typed benefits can increase the attractiveness of gender-atypical occupations for female participants. Female participants who consider atypical occupations place relatively higher value on these benefits and tend to exhibit less traditionally feminine preferences. We also find suggestive evidence that anticipated social reactions, particularly from parents, accompany these choices.

59ec699e9f:2934120f38330147.title: Religion Versus Religiosity: What Matters for Hiring?
59ec699e9f:2934120f38330147.author: Baert, Stijn
59ec699e9f:2934120f38330147.summary: Religious discrimination in hiring is rarely studied independently from ethnic discrimination. We fill this gap using a preregistered factorial survey experiment in which professional recruiters evaluate candidate profiles that independently vary by ethnic majority versus minority names, visual religious signals, and volunteering activities signalling either Christian or Muslim religious affiliation. Beyond hiring intentions, we measure recruitersâ€™, colleaguesâ€™, and customersâ€™ anticipated willingness to work with candidates, as well as recruitersâ€™ HEXACO personality assessments of the candidates. Candidates whose religious position recruiters identify receive lower interview ratings than candidates whose position remains unclear to them, and this penalty does not differ between Christian, Muslim, and atheist attributions; interview propensity declines further as attributed religiosity rises; and among the assigned signals, only religious volunteering reduces hiring chances. Religious candidates are not regarded as less diligent or less honest, but as less likely to be accepted by others.

59ec699e9f:06c77b4b9eef9aab.title: GLP-1 Treatment and Work Capacity
59ec699e9f:06c77b4b9eef9aab.author: Sergio Galletta
59ec699e9f:06c77b4b9eef9aab.summary: Using linked Finnish administrative records and a staggered difference-in-differences design, we estimate how starting semaglutide (Ozempic) affects work capacity, measured by medically certified sickness absence. The first purchase is followed by persistent use and improved glycemic control, indicating that recorded purchases correspond to sustained and clinically active treatment. The reduction in sickness absence is near zero during months 0–5, becomes progressively larger thereafter, and is largest during months 12–18. Averaged over event months 0–18, sickness allowance receipt falls by 16.9 percent and compensated days by 14.3 percent relative to pre-treatment means. The decline in full-day sickness absence is not offset by greater reliance on unemployment or partial sickness benefits. The results show that semaglutide improves work capacity and can generate economic benefits beyond its direct effects on metabolic health.

59ec699e9f:e1d0a860f381ab05.title: How to Increase the Mental Well-Being of Your Employees? An Overview of Research Testing Interventions in the Workplace
59ec699e9f:e1d0a860f381ab05.author: Baert, Stijn
59ec699e9f:e1d0a860f381ab05.summary: This systematic literature review provides a state-of-the-art overview of the effectiveness of workplace interventions aimed at improving workersâ€™ mental well-being. Specifically, it examines which types of interventions are effective for which aspects of mental well-being, both in the short and long term. To this end, we identify 125 randomised controlled trials comprising 147 interventions that vary in their objectives (prevention, treatment, or reintegration), targets (workers or work), methods (cognitive, meditation-based, physical, ergonomic, organisational, or multimethod) and delivery channels (offline, online or hybrid). Mental well-being outcomes are classified as biological and self-reported indicators of the three components of subjective mental well-being (evaluative, affective, and eudaimonic well-being). Overall, we find that, for preventing and treating early mental health symptoms, cognitive or meditation-based interventions targeting personal coping resources appear most promising. In contrast, successful reintegration seems to require a combination of cognitive and organisational interventions, with the latter addressing job demands and resources.

59ec699e9f:1d01c428371127e6.title: A competitive world
59ec699e9f:1d01c428371127e6.author: Tungodden, Bertil
59ec699e9f:1d01c428371127e6.summary: We provide globally representative evidence on two attitudes toward competition: individuals’ willingness to compete and the importance they attach to boys and girls being willing to compete, using a novel survey module that we fielded as part of the 2022 Gallup World Poll. The data cover more than 66, 000 individuals across 62 countries. Men are more willing to compete than women in all but two countries, and willingness to compete is higher among younger, more educated, and higher-income individuals. Attitudes toward children’s willingness to compete vary substantially across countries, with competitiveness valued more for boys in some countries and for girls in others. Both attitudes are systematically related to the economic and social environment. Individuals exposed to greater inequality or faster population growth during their formative years are more willing to compete and place greater importance on children being willing to compete. Greater exposure to gender equality during formative years is associated with smaller gender gaps in both adults’ willingness to compete and attitudes toward the competitiveness of boys and girls. Our findings reveal striking global regularities while highlighting the role of the social environment in shaping attitudes toward competition.

59ec699e9f:2cf24bcb7e8bda5a.title: Labor share, FDI and Productivity
59ec699e9f:2cf24bcb7e8bda5a.author: Krekó, Judit
59ec699e9f:2cf24bcb7e8bda5a.summary: This paper examines how foreign direct investment affects the labor share through productivity differences between foreign- and domestically owned firms. We develop a search-and-matching model in which more productive foreign firms acquire domestic firms. Foreign ownership raises productivity and wages, but incomplete pass-through of the productivity advantage to workers reduces the labor share. Using European industry-level data, we find that greater foreign employment penetration is associated with lower labor shares and that the foreign productivity premium substantially exceeds the foreign wage premium. Hungarian administrative firm data show the same pattern: foreign-owned firms have higher productivity and labor costs but lower labor shares. Event-study estimates around foreign acquisitions are less precise but are consistent with this mechanism at longer horizons. Our results show how economies with a large foreign-owned sector can combine relatively high wages with relatively low labor shares and highlight persistent foreign–domestic productivity differences as a potential explanation for labor-share differences across Europe.

59ec699e9f:349e7186d4483924.title: Carbon Taxation, Firm Performance, and Labor Demand
59ec699e9f:349e7186d4483924.author: Karlsson, Jimmy
59ec699e9f:349e7186d4483924.summary: Carbon taxation is one of the main policy instruments for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, yet there is still limited evidence on its effects on firms and workers. This paper studies the environmental and economic effects of carbon taxation, with a particular focus on heterogeneity in labor demand across worker groups. I exploit a reform that increased the effective carbon tax for a subset of Swedish manufacturing firms between 2011 and 2018, and combine administrative firm data with matched employer-employee records in a difference-in-differences design. The reform reduced emissions by about 30%, primarily through substitution away from fossil fuels toward biofuels and district heating. It also reduced revenue and employment, with the strongest negative effects concentrated among emission-intensive firms. The employment effects are driven mainly by older workers without a high school degree, although older, highly educated workers are also negatively affected in the most exposed firms. Additional evidence suggests that firms adjusted labor demand primarily through lower hiring rather than higher separations. Scaled by the average increase in effective tax rates (measured in euro per ton CO2), the estimates imply semi-elasticities of -0.58% for emissions and -0.20% for employment among low-educated workers. These results suggest that carbon taxation can substantially reduce industrial emissions, but with concentrated labor-market costs.

59ec699e9f:f8ae0c16a535be81.title: Permanent residency policy and skilled immigration: Evidence from a Swedish reform
59ec699e9f:f8ae0c16a535be81.author: Lundberg, Erik
59ec699e9f:f8ae0c16a535be81.summary: Aging populations and labor shortages in skill-intensive sectors have led many countries to pursue targeted policies to attract international talent. We study a migration reform in Sweden that offered international doctoral students from outside the EU an easier path to permanent residency. Implemented in 2014, the reform shortened the required period of residence from eight to four years, allowed these students to obtain permanent residency immediately after graduation, and granted their spouses a work permit during their doctoral studies. Using the European students as a comparison group in a difference-in-differences design, we find that the treated international students are 10.5 pp (18%) more likely to stay in Sweden three years after graduation. Higher settlement prospects also increase their language investments and marriage rates during the PhD. These effects are larger for cohorts that have longer exposure to the reform and for those who carry out their doctoral research in STEM. In addition, the reform raises both employment and language investments among the partners of the treated international students. Taken together, the policy increases permanent residency among international graduates as well as leads them and their families to make long-term choices conducive to integration. Finally, using a shift-share design, where we combine the reform with the pre-existing variation in the share of international students across research fields, we find positive peer effects on residency. More international students settling in Sweden increases the probability of their European peers making the same choice.

59ec699e9f:605aeb37cee5fef9.title: Beyond the Unemployment Rate: A Structural Labor Market Indicator
59ec699e9f:605aeb37cee5fef9.author: Damjan Pfajfar
59ec699e9f:605aeb37cee5fef9.summary: Labor market variables frequently send conflicting signals about the degree of slack or tightness, often complicating policy assessments at critical junctures. This paper develops a Structural Labor Market Indicator (SLMI) for the U.S. economy that addresses the limitations of existing univariate measures or atheoretical statistical approaches that synthesize multiple labor market indicators but cannot distinguish between supply and demand driving forces. We construct the SLMI using a medium scale New Keynesian DSGE model featuring search and matching frictions, endogenous labor force participation, and variable hours. The model is disciplined by a comprehensive dataset that includes not only labor market variables but also other macroeconomic aggregates. The SLMI synthesizes model-implied gaps across multiple labor market dimensions using principal component analysis. We show that GDP growth and inflation provide substantial information about labor market slack beyond what labor market variables contain, validating our multi-variable structural approach. Relative to alternative measures, the SLMI often provides earlier warnings of deteriorating conditions at recession onset but recovers more gradually during expansions.

59ec699e9f:bab2c540887d0eca.title: Spatial mobility and the risk of dropping out of vocational education and training in Germany: Costs, resources, and returns
59ec699e9f:bab2c540887d0eca.author: Wicht, Alexandra
59ec699e9f:bab2c540887d0eca.summary: Vocational education and training (VET) dropout disrupts school-to-work transitions. While spatial mobility is an important strategy for accessing VET, little is known about how it relates to subsequent dropout. Drawing on a cost-benefit perspective, this study examines whether first-year VET dropout differs by spatial mobility and whether these differences vary with resources available to bear mobility-related costs and returns that may offset them. We use representative longitudinal data from the German National Educational Panel Study linked to administrative geospatial data. Logistic regression models distinguish non-mobile students from those mobile within and between regional labor markets (RLMs) and assess heterogeneity by parental socioeconomic status (SES), VET wages, realized occupational aspirations, regional attractiveness, and regional person-environment match. Predicted dropout probabilities are approximately three percentage points higher for mobility within RLMs and four points higher for mobility between RLMs than for no mobility. These mobility-related differences decrease with increasing parental SES for both mobility types. Higher VET wages correspond to smaller dropout differences for mobility within RLMs, whereas greater realization of occupational aspirations corresponds to smaller differences for mobility between RLMs. Higher regional attractiveness shows a similar pattern only for mobility within RLMs, while higher regional person-environment match coincides with smaller dropout differences for both mobility types. Overall, mobility-related dropout differences vary with available resources and realized returns. The social patterning of mobility-related dropout differences may contribute to inequalities in school-to-work transitions, underscoring the importance of considering spatial mobility and regional contexts in research on youths’ educational decision-making.

59ec699e9f:ec357d3932d02e7b.title: When Is the Mover-Design Event Study Coefficient a Place-Effect Share?
59ec699e9f:ec357d3932d02e7b.author: Vahid Moghani
59ec699e9f:ec357d3932d02e7b.summary: Mover-design event studies are a leading approach to separating place effects from sorting. The coefficient is often interpreted as the share of cross-sectional variation in location means due to places. I show the coefficient depends on how movers connect locations: two economies can be identical in place effects, sorting, and location means, yet deliver different mover coefficients. Only under directional isotropy, a testable condition, does the coefficient permit a cross-sectional reading: it averages the variance share of place effects and the share that equalizing them removes. An illustration in Dutch employerâ€“employee wage data rejects the condition.

59ec699e9f:0381cb4524899e6a.title: The Cost of Women's Labor Supply and Occupational Choice Frictions
59ec699e9f:0381cb4524899e6a.author: Arato, Hiroki
59ec699e9f:0381cb4524899e6a.summary: This paper quantifies women's occupational choice frictions between manufacturing and services in Japan from the early 2000s to the late 2010s using a general equilibrium Roy model. We then decompose changes in women's sectoral employment propensities relative to men's into comparative-advantage and friction components. In the full sample (ages 20–59), the model-implied occupational distortion moves closer to the frictionless benchmark, whereas in the young subsample (ages 20–34), it shifts from manufacturing-biased to service-biased by the late 2010s. Over the same period, women's comparative disadvantage in manufacturing narrows, especially in the young subsample. Within the model, changes in comparative advantage and occupational choice frictions largely offset each other, so women's sectoral employment propensities relative to men's change only modestly. Counterfactual simulations show that output losses from occupational choice frictions evolve differently across the two samples: they decline sharply in the full sample but increase in the young subsample. Specifically, the output loss falls from about 18% to about 4% in the full sample, whereas it rises from about 6% to about 10% in the young subsample.

59ec699e9f:12b1fbb9671761bc.title: Intangible Capital, Markups, and Markdowns: Evidence from Japanese Listed Firms
59ec699e9f:12b1fbb9671761bc.author: YAMAMOTO, Yohei
59ec699e9f:12b1fbb9671761bc.summary: This paper examines how intangible capital is related to firms' market power in product and labor markets using an unbalanced panel of Japanese listed firms from 1980 to 2024. We estimate firm-level markups and markdowns following the production-function approaches employed by the standard literature and then relate these measures to two types of intangible capital: R&D stock and organizational capital. The empirical results show that organizational capital is positively associated with markups and negatively associated with markdowns, while the role of R&D stock is relatively limited and less robust. These findings suggest that organizational capital may strengthen firms' product-market position while also encouraging rent sharing with workers. The stagnant accumulation of organizational capital may therefore help explain why Japan experienced weak price and wage growth since the 2000s.

4a32a2255e:c915fbf11c3ceae5.title: The Geography of Life Chances and Intergenerational Mobility
4a32a2255e:c915fbf11c3ceae5.author: Connor, Dylan Shane
4a32a2255e:c915fbf11c3ceae5.summary: We have entered a new era of soaring inequalities in income and wealth, patterns driven by a highly differentiated landscape of opportunity. This economic reality has propelled the geographies of intergenerational mobility and life chances to the forefront of the social science agenda. While geographers are increasingly engaging with these topics, the field of economic geography provides a critical, yet underutilized, theoretical foundation for this work. This chapter proposes the People-Experience-Places (PEP) framework, a model for analyzing the geographic differentiation of life chances across space and time. Drawing from core schools of thought within economic geography, the framework identifies the foundational mechanisms that produce spatially differentiated opportunity regimes and their impact on intergenerational mobility. The chapter concludes with a call for economic geographers to return to the core concerns of understanding and addressing inequalities in livelihood possibilities.

4a32a2255e:581561d3d3520369.title: The Geographic and Sectoral Impact of Productivity
4a32a2255e:581561d3d3520369.author: Del Valle Fuentes, Miguel Angel
4a32a2255e:581561d3d3520369.summary: To understand the geographic and sectoral impact of productivity, we build the first input-output matrix disaggregated at the geographic level within a country using unique administrative data harmonized to match national accounts. We use this data from Chile to calibrate a state-of-the-art general equilibrium quantitative trade model with production networks, labor mobility, firm selection, international and domestic trade, congestion of fixed factors, and knowledge diffusion. We consider two applications. First, we study the aggregate effects of local productivity shocks. We show that location-sector interactions are crucial: locations and sectors separately account for less than half of the dispersion in GDP elasticities from location-sector- specific productivity shocks. Geography-specific input-output linkages explain 16% of the dispersion, due to the role played by small and influential markets. Second, we analyze the exit of a large steel plant. We show that geographically disaggregated production linkages substantially increase the propagation of the plant exit.

4a32a2255e:f12807b3380a05fe.title: Estimating Regional Industry Employment from Economic Location Mechanisms: A Constrained Spatial Disaggregation for European Geographies
4a32a2255e:f12807b3380a05fe.author: Boero, Riccardo
4a32a2255e:f12807b3380a05fe.summary: Fine-scale employment by industry is largely unavailable across European municipalities, yet it underpins regional economic analysis, environmental-economic extensions, and the regionalization of input--output accounts. This paper presents a mechanism-driven, constrained spatial disaggregation framework that estimates industry employment down to the Local Administrative Unit level while preserving official totals exactly at every geographical level. The economic mechanisms that shape where activity locates --- settlement, infrastructure and accessibility, natural-resource endowments, and inter-industry co-location --- are represented as a reproducible input dataset assembled from official and remote-sensing sources; a family of constrained allocation models, combined by a cross-validated convex ensemble, is trained on data-rich United States geographies and transferred to Europe under official Eurostat totals as constraints. Validated against independent national statistics in Italy, France, Germany, and Spain, the estimates reproduce the observed spatial distribution of employment within the held-out uncertainty of the models themselves, and the error does not inflate down the four-step disaggregation. The framework is open, inspectable, and reproducible, providing internally consistent fine-scale employment estimates wherever sub-national industry data are sparse.

4a32a2255e:9fed8a98586b464a.title: Agglomeration and Fragility: Firm Responses to the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
4a32a2255e:9fed8a98586b464a.author: Eric Strobl
4a32a2255e:9fed8a98586b464a.summary: In this paper we investigate how the disruption of local agglomeration economies affects firm adjustment following a catastrophic urban disaster. To this end we digitalized a unique survey of firms in Tokyo City completed shortly after the earthquake and before any government reconstruction intervention. Using detailed information on the damage experienced by firms and the main good that they produced, as well as where they were located, we construct measures of losses of local agglomeration economies by identifying firms that either permanently ceased operation or relocated elsewhere. To identify causal impacts we exploit plausibly exogenous variation in fire destruction generated by the interaction between fire outbreak locations and local wind direction and speed immediately after the earthquake. Our econometrics results show that a loss of agglomeration economies as a result of the earthquake had a substantial impact on firms shutting down or relocating, with average effects of 13 and 11 per cent for these outcomes, respectively.

4a32a2255e:ea5b5b61b8ec50ed.title: When London Burned to Sticks: The Economic Impact of the Great Fire of 1666
4a32a2255e:ea5b5b61b8ec50ed.author: Tsoukli, Xanthi
4a32a2255e:ea5b5b61b8ec50ed.summary: This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the Great Fireâ€™s effects on Londonâ€™s economic geography. Our analysis reveals both continuity and change. There was a swift postfire recovery accompanied by some shift in economic activity towards the City of Westminster by 1690, with markets spreading outside the City, but financial services largely remaining inside. Analysis of London Hearth Tax records further illustrates a significant change in the wealth distribution, with wealthier households returning to fire-impacted areas, reshaping the cityâ€™s housing and social structure.

33e1d7779a:ea817bb0c169f857.title: Khanna, Massie say they can force another Epstein vote

Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky. ) announced Thursday they've secured commitments for the 218 signatures needed to force another vote the release of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . The big picture: Answers about the disgraced financier and his web of wealthy connections have continued to haunt the administration, with Attorney General Todd Blanche now facing the threat of contempt proceedings over the Epstein files. This is the bipartisan duo's second push in less than a year after they forced their first Epstein transparency bill through Congress, which the president signed after initially opposing the effort. Driving the news: " Thomas Massie and I have defied history for a second time," Khanna said in a video posted to social media late Thursday afternoon. His post read that the pair had secured commitments for 218 votes on their discharge petition, including from three Republicans: Reps. Ralph Norman (R-S.C), Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.). Two Democrats were sick, he added, but will sign the day the House returns. Massie also posted that he and his partner across the aisle would have enough names once lawmakers are back from a lengthy recess. Friction point: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) dumped fuel on the fire blazing between him and Massie by again sending the House home early this week, Axios' Kate Santaliz reports. The more than six-week recess will also delay Massie's effort to force a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Johnson's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What's inside: Massie and Khanna introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II in July to strengthen enforcement of last year's law. It would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the U.S. attorney general over alleged unlawful withholdings, redactions or failure to produce records. The bill would also require the attorney general provide certain unredacted…

33e1d7779a:8ca764ff78e4a2da.title: Why Sydney Sweeney's nude ad struck such a nerve with women athletes
33e1d7779a:8ca764ff78e4a2da.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:8ca764ff78e4a2da.summary: A sports-betting ad featuring a semi-nude Sydney Sweeney triggered a backlash across women's sports , with female athletes flooding social media with a countermessage: This is what women in sports actually look like. The big picture: Ads have long sexualized women, but the Novig ad's appeal to the male gaze hit differently at a moment when female athletes have cultural cachet and the platforms to push back. Driving the news: Highlight reels of women diving , pitching , tackling , shredding , lifting , skating , sprinting , leaping and covering sports have flooded social media this week — all with the same core message. British sprinter Amy Hunt delivered that refrain on-air this week, smiling and out of breath after the World Athletics Ultimate Championship: "Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like: 21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears," referring to American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time . Women's sports are in an era of rapid momentum: The NCAA reported record high women's participation earlier this year, while Bank of America predicted U.S. women's sports revenue will grow more than 250% by 2030. There's still a long way to go on screen time, says Purdue University professor Cheryl Cooky, who studies sports and gender. But she says traditional media increasingly covers women's sports more seriously. Still, Cooky says , "it's in some ways not surprising that we get [the] Sydney Sweeney ad at this moment," describing it as "part of a backlash to the kinds of gains that women's sports, and by proxy, women more generally, are making in our society." Some online argued the ad wasn't meant to portray a female athlete and was instead targeting sports bettors, who are more likely to be men. But Cooky says it still struck a nerve because "we thought we were past the point of having to make a case that women in sport contexts are not simply sexual objects for male consumption." Between the lines: Even if traditional media has made…

33e1d7779a:7b9978e96806ff7f.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
33e1d7779a:7b9978e96806ff7f.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:7b9978e96806ff7f.summary: Warren Buffett will step down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, less than a year after handing over the CEO reins, the company said Friday. The big picture: The "Oracle of Omaha" is 96, and his insurance-to-railroads conglomerate is moving onto a new generation, with his son Howard as chairman. This is breaking news. Check back for updates.

33e1d7779a:c6a48162b431516b.title: Oil's shrug emoji era
33e1d7779a:c6a48162b431516b.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:c6a48162b431516b.summary: And the award for honesty in oil market analysis goes to ... J.P. Morgan! "For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don't have a baseline view. We simply don't know how to model the endgame ," bank researchers said in a note (emphasis added). Why it matters: While the phrasing is unusually blunt, the sentiment is shared to varying degrees . Market watchers have come to grips with the likelihood that the status of the Strait of Hormuz — and the number of barrels getting through — will be messy for months to come. The big picture: At the outset of the Iran war, J.P. Morgan's "Oil Markets Weekly" crew assumed there were "economic red lines" the White House would not cross. The list includes $100 oil; gasoline near $5 per gallon; and 10-year Treasury yields hitting 5% (higher levels raise borrowing costs). And yet: "Six months later, many of those lines have been crossed, yet the exit strategy is less clear, not more." The intrigue: The ongoing disruption of Middle East barrels, even if Hormuz transit has risen in recent weeks, will keep eroding the market's shock absorbers. That said, lower oil demand has done more work than expected to ease stress on supplies, which has enabled a slower drawdown of countries' oil stockpiles, the J.P. Morgan note argues. So "fears of inventories being close to exhausted as a balancing mechanism are premature," and there's an ample cushion to keep prices relatively contained "for now." Yes, but: Even if crude prices haven't soared as high as many predicted when the strait was first choked off, soaring energy costs and shortages are creating pain, anger and unrest in many nations worldwide, the New York Times reports. What we're watching: Uncertainty is also affecting dealmaking. Elevated yet volatile prices are shaking up mergers and acquisitions in the exploration and production sector, per the consultancy Rystad Energy. The conflict has "acted as both a headwind and a tailwind," a new note states. High prices are…

33e1d7779a:cd70e15aa345b720.title: "The Axios Show": Hasan Piker wants to campaign for AOC in 2028
33e1d7779a:cd70e15aa345b720.author: Alex Thompson
33e1d7779a:cd70e15aa345b720.summary: Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker said he "absolutely" wants to campaign for New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez if she runs for president in 2028 and said he has talked with AOC and her team, he said in the new episode of "The Axios Show." Why it matters: Piker, who has millions of followers online, has been a high-profile campaign surrogate this year for a new generation of left-wing candidates, and wants to do the same in 2028. Driving the news: Despite Piker's ambitions, some Democratic politicians have begun distancing themselves from him because of his controversial commentary. Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's Democratic nominee for the Senate, campaigned with Piker during the Senate primary. But after Piker told Axios that he believed America's long history of attacks in the Middle East that have killed civilians made it worse than al-Qaeda "pound for pound," El-Sayed said he disagreed and that Piker didn't speak for his campaign. El-Sayed has said Piker won't appear with him in the final weeks of the race before the Nov. 3 election. In an hour-long interview with Axios, Piker explained his worldview and defended his stances that some Democrats are distancing themselves from: China: Piker traveled to China last year and has said that the country is the closest government model he would like to see adopted in the U.S. He also thinks that "trajectory-wise, I worry that a Chinese child might have better conditions in the next decade or next two decades than an American one. And I think that should worry every American citizen." Asked about his past praise of Mao Zedong, Piker said "he's a great man of history. Of course, there were a lot of excesses." When asked to clarify what he meant as "excesses," Piker said: "Deaths borne out of mismanagement and famine." Political violence: Axios asked Piker about several of his past statements about killing or harming political opponents, and he said they amounted to "three or four choice quotes." He said he consistently says…

33e1d7779a:5362d8f082d16f5b.title: Inside the scramble for trusted AI cops
33e1d7779a:5362d8f082d16f5b.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:5362d8f082d16f5b.summary: A host of industry players, policy wonks and businesses are grappling with the question of how to regulate AI in a trustworthy manner. Inside the White House, it's mostly business as usual. Why it matters: The industry's mad dash is the product of an ad hoc regulatory apparatus and a general consensus that swift action from Washington is unlikely in the near term . State of play: AI CEOs have been grappling with how to test advanced AI and work with Beijing on safety standards, while the White House favors a solution where the industry finds ways to police itself. That means the race is on to decide who will be anointed as third-party evaluators of AI systems and controls as the companies await legislation or White House action beyond the current voluntary process. A robust ecosystem of safety and benchmarking groups already exists, but some White House officials and AI execs see them as too closely tied to top AI companies. Other options include businesses and startups that already do evaluations, as well as some more unorthodox suggestions. What they're saying: Companies have the most expertise when it comes to AI and understand what the White House's AI voluntary framework requires, according to a White House official. "These people are not 12-year-olds," the official said. "The top frontier companies need to come to a consensus on what they want because they haven't agreed on anything," the official continued. "If these companies feel it's such a dire situation, they have every right, reason, and ability to throttle their models." Friction point: Some third-party evaluators — including individuals at METR, which investigated the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — have been singled out for having close ties to the effective altruism movement , as well as to companies they would be policing. One of the lead outside investigators of the Hugging Face episode is married to Paul Christiano , a seasoned AI safety and technology official who recently joined the board of…

33e1d7779a:f152572142e824af.title: Exclusive: Scalise puts GOP high-water mark at 225 House seats
33e1d7779a:f152572142e824af.author: Hans Nichols
33e1d7779a:f152572142e824af.summary: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) is staring at a scary political environment for Republicans and claiming to see something very different: a path to 225 seats . Why it matters: Republican leaders insist they can retain the majority, but only if they drive their voters to the polls by manufacturing the kind of voter enthusiasm Democrats are generating organically. "If we make it a contrast election, we win," Scalise told Axios in an interview Thursday. "We could get to 225. It would be a good night for us if we did, but it's possible," he said. "235 is not," he said. "You're literally doing coin tosses in a couple of seats." Between the lines: Asked if he saw any signs of a blue wave forming or the map expanding, Scalise said: "Not right now. No." Reality check: Republicans know that history — and many of the indicators heading into November — is working against them. "I know what history says, you know, but history's not on the ballot," Scalise said. Still, Democrats are turning out in primaries — and special elections — as if they're getting free gas cards for showing up. Democrats lead by nearly nine percentage points on the generic ballot. President Trump's approval rating is below 40%, according to the RealClearPolitics average . And Trump is underwater by a whopping 61 percentage points on inflation in a recent poll, an apparent record . Zoom in: Republicans are examining the map with a jeweler's loupe and insist the picture isn't as bleak in the pivotal battleground seats. "We're not looking at national polls; we go district by district," Scalise said. That means trench warfare in 35 seats, where Republicans say they have proven winners, plenty of money and new rules to spend it . "We've got 20 [seats] on our side that we're fighting to hold on to that are real competitive, and 15 [seats] that we have a real chance to flip," he said. "These are knock-down, drag-out fights." What we're hearing: The White House has long thought of the midterms as a…

33e1d7779a:84f4338235feabf7.title: Scoop: Trump expected to meet with Venezuela's new leader
33e1d7779a:84f4338235feabf7.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:84f4338235feabf7.summary: President Trump is making plans for a first-ever meeting with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, as early as next week, sources familiar with the discussions tell Axios. Why it matters: The potential meeting showcases the close relations between the nations under Trump. But it's also fraught with political risks that extend from Miami to Caracas. Driving the news: Trump is already planning to meet with Gulf leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York next week to discuss the Iran War, and those who know his thinking say he wants to make time for a sidelines sit-down with Rodriguez as early as Tuesday, sources said. "Iran is tough, but Venezuela is without a doubt the president's top success and Delcy is a key to that," a Trump adviser said. "Unless something goes really wrong, the president wants to make time." A senior administration official cautioned: "Nothing is finalized. This is up to the president." On Sunday, when asked about meeting Rodriguez, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that "I may be, I may be." Zoom in: The New York City meeting could happen just blocks from the federal lockup where Rodriguez's predecessor and onetime ally, socialist Nicolas Maduro, awaits trial on narco-terrorism charges. Maduro was seized Jan. 3 in Caracas in a U.S. military operation authorized by Trump. Rodriguez assumed power after the coup and has worked closely with Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to normalize relations between the countries, including the inking of a massive but controversial Venezuelan oil deal first reported by Axios. Friction point: Clustered in South Florida, conservative and vocal Venezuelan exile community has expressed increasing agitation with the administration for working so closely with Rodriguez, a lifelong socialist who rose to power along with Maduro under strongman Hugo Chavez, both foes of the U.S. this century. Adding to the anger in the diaspora: neither Trump nor Rubio has called for elections in…

33e1d7779a:8f1400af0d07a784.title: Inside House Democrats' behind-the-scenes food fight
33e1d7779a:8f1400af0d07a784.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:8f1400af0d07a784.summary: The House's last in-session week before the midterms was beset by furious private finger-pointing between House Democrats following several high-profile rebellions . Why it matters: This dynamic may only worsen if Democrats retake the House, which is set to see an influx of distinctly rebellious and independent lawmakers , particularly on the left. There is even chatter among members contrasting the ability of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to control members with that of his top deputy, Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), according to two House Democrats. Said one of the lawmakers, speaking on the condition of anonymity to share details of sensitive private discussions: "People are talking about 'mom and dad'. … Dad is soft." "I think people are asking the question: If this is happening in the minority, are you prepared for what will happen in the majority?" said a third House Democrat. "There is no daylight between the three of us," Jeffries said at a Thursday press conference with Clark and Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.). "We'll address the situation when we address the situation," he added. A Democratic leadership aide told Axios that everything Jeffries' deputies do is in coordination with him and doesn't represent a break between leaders. Driving the news: Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Jared Golden (D-Maine) on Tuesday provided Republican leadership with the necessary votes to advance a package of GOP bills, including a Russia sanctions bill strongly opposed by Democratic leaders. It was the second time this month the pair of centrists defected from leadership on a procedural vote — even after Clark and Jeffries publicly threatened them with punishment the first time. "People thought the first time was a mistake. The second time is defiance," said a fourth House Democrat, telling Axios the two "operate like they are above the caucus." Clark, along with Jeffries, engaged Gluesenkamp Perez in a heated…

33e1d7779a:f49f1c541d3f61c5.title: RFK Jr. questions vaccine safety at anti-vaccine organization gathering
33e1d7779a:f49f1c541d3f61c5.author: Caitlin Owens
33e1d7779a:f49f1c541d3f61c5.summary: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday returned to the the anti-vaccine group he founded, using a keynote address to signal the Trump administration isn't done questioning the safety of routine shots and expanding carveouts to federal mandates. Why it matters: Though Kennedy avoided some of his most politically incendiary rhetoric, the speech made clear that the Department of Health and Human Services is working hard behind the scenes to continue reshaping federal vaccine policy. He again questioned the safety of routine childhood vaccines and asserted they play a role in the development of chronic illnesses — questions that ignore decades of science supporting the vaccines' safety. Driving the news: Kennedy spoke for more than an hour Thursday afternoon at a Children's Health Defense meeting in Washington, D.C., highlighting the Trump administration's work on healthy food before turning to vaccines. He listed what the federal government is doing to reverse, in vaccine critics' eyes, decades of negligence on the issue. And Kennedy assured the audience that President Trump is fully committed to the cause. "He's directed us to pursue answers to strengthen vaccine safety, to expand options for families who want them and to preserve individual choice without federal mandates," Kennedy said. "Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House." Between the lines: Kennedy addressed those frustrated with the administration's pace, in a nod to Make America Healthy Again movement members who feel he hasn't done enough to crack down on vaccines. "In government, a bunch of things have to happen before something else happens, or you get sued, and it's a very laborious system, and there's a lot of inertia built in," he said. "If we were able to overcome it, we would have changed things on day one, but those would have been short lived and I would have been out of a job." He certainly didn't sound like someone who's ready to leave office…

33e1d7779a:dbb59960b3df41f6.title: Judge steps in as Kennedy Center demolition fears grow
33e1d7779a:dbb59960b3df41f6.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:dbb59960b3df41f6.summary: Trump officials must give 30 days' written notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center "including but not limited to any ' demolition '" of the main building, a federal judge ruled Thursday. Why it matters: The ruling reinforces an earlier injunction blocking the Kennedy Center from closing for its planned renovation, after President Trump and administration officials raised the possibility of demolishing the building. The ruling allows the center to continue making "emergency repairs" rather than halt them entirely. Driving the news: District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled Thursday that the defendants must file a "detailed status report, supported by a sworn declaration from a knowledgeable representative of the Kennedy Center, on the 'temporary closure' and emergency repairs described" in the Kennedy Center board's most recent court filing, per a minute order published Thursday. Representatives for the White House and Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: Trump said on social media Tuesday that the center was going to be closed. Shortly after, an announcement played over the center's loudspeakers telling attendees that it was closed. Legal counsel for the institution initially said someone had improperly triggered a fire alarm, causing the loudspeaker announcement. But when the plaintiff's staff attempted to enter Wednesday during regular operating hours, security denied them entry and said the building was closed for interior construction and safety reasons. The staff member said she later saw workers using forklifts to bring in additional construction-style gates and watched a forklift carrying permanent fencing repeatedly strike the building's structural pillars. Context: Trump was recently pictured looking at a markup reading, "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." He told reporters on Wednesday that the Kennedy Center had been bleeding money before he "got involved." "For the Trump administration, for me,…

33e1d7779a:66f9e6ecfb824689.title: Fear and loathing in Trump's Miami backyard over immigration crackdown
33e1d7779a:66f9e6ecfb824689.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:66f9e6ecfb824689.summary: Staring into the camera, Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) cut a new campaign ad that told President Trump what so many of her fellow Hispanic Republicans in Miami are saying: Immigration crackdown has gone too far. Why it matters: The anger at Trump over heavy-handed immigration enforcement is palpable in Miami-Dade County, and there's mounting political worry among Republicans across the state that it could cost the GOP in the midterm elections. Zoom in: A bellwether, Miami-Dade is Florida's most-populous county, which Trump flipped to the Republican column in 2020 and 2024 thanks to strong Latino support, especially among Cuban Americans. "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in her ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today." Trump carried her district by 15 points two years ago. Today, she's tied in polls with newscaster Eliot Rodriguez, a fellow Cuban American, who said her new ad was a sign of desperation. A Trump adviser told Axios: "I'm getting the Trumpiest Cubans sending me videos from Miami of guys getting busted at places like the gas station, for no apparent reason." By the numbers: In Miami-Dade, 62% of the county's 1.3 million registered voters are Hispanic. They account for 76% of the registered Republicans. 63% of Hispanic voters said they supported "deporting illegal immigrants" while 34% were opposed to them, according to a poll conducted last month by a GOP pollster and shared with Axios But those numbers switched when it came to how deportations were being carried out: Just 29% were in favor; 58% were opposed. "The support is just evaporating. The economy sucks and ICE is just out of control," said the pollster, who's from Miami. "People feel they didn't sign up for this." Yes, but: Trump ran on a platform of mass deportations. He promised to target undocumented criminals, but the president's critics warned that his aggressive immigration push…

33e1d7779a:bc87ae5ffc1e3cfd.title: White House pulls ICE nominee who drew MAGA pushback
33e1d7779a:bc87ae5ffc1e3cfd.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:bc87ae5ffc1e3cfd.summary: The White House is pulling Lance Schroyer's stalled nomination to lead ICE. The big picture: Schroyer's limited immigration experience created tension between Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and border czar Tom Homan, along with other MAGA figures, Axios' Brittany Gibson reported last month. Driving the news: The White House did not explain why it withdrew the nomination of Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state highway trooper. Schroyer was also formerly part of Mullin's security detail . Catch up quick: Trump announced Schroyer's nomination in June, saying he "has what it takes to DETAIN AND DEPORT Illegal Alien Criminals." He urged the Senate to "CONFIRM Lance, IMMEDIATELY" — but that didn't happen. David Venturella, who previously worked for a private prison operator, is the current acting ICE director. Friction point: Schroyer would've taken over a multi-billion dollar budget, inflated under the Trump administration, and a sprawling immigration crackdown that's triggered mass protests , lawsuits and due process concerns . Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) threatened to delay Schroyer's confirmation hearing until he received more information about the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota earlier this year, The Wall Street Journal reported last month. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:b5e53cd25aebe257.title: Blanche warned of contempt risk in Epstein files case
33e1d7779a:b5e53cd25aebe257.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:b5e53cd25aebe257.summary: A federal judge warned Attorney General Todd Blanche Wednesday that he could face contempt proceedings if the Department of Justice fails to comply with an order involving the release or review of Epstein files. Why it matters: The case could force DOJ to release additional Epstein records or remove redactions that a court determines aren't permitted under the law. What they're saying: U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan wrote in a 20-page order Wednesday that a civil contempt charge would be "premature" for now, but warned it could become appropriate if Blanche fails to comply with the court's renewed order. "[C]ourts have the inherent power to enforce compliance with their lawful orders through civil contempt," Sullivan wrote. "A contempt finding is proper where 'the putative contemnor has violated an order that is clear and unambiguous' and the violation of an order is 'proved by clear and convincing evidence.'" Catch up quick: Independent journalist Katie Phang brought the lawsuit, alleging the DOJ hasn't released all documents required under the Epstein Files Transparency Act , which Congress passed last November. Sullivan said last month he didn't want to start contempt proceedings, but added that the public "has a right to know what the hell is going on in this case" and the "victims have a right to know and the court has a right to know." Zoom in: Sullivan ruled Wednesday that the DOJ provided adequate documentation showing some email redactions were made to protect survivors' privacy. But he said the department hadn't provided enough documentation to justify redactions in other emails and ordered it to provide additional documentation for private in camera review — a process in which a judge reviews confidential, sensitive or privileged documents outside public view. The judge rejected the DOJ's assertion that handwritten FBI notes were "properly withheld because they are 'substantially similar to' and therefore duplicative of the typewritten reports." He…

33e1d7779a:7b7dca8cc8117197.title: Trump tells Axios he's approaching major crossroads in Iran war
33e1d7779a:7b7dca8cc8117197.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:7b7dca8cc8117197.summary: President Trump told Axios Thursday that he's approaching a critical juncture in the Iran war over whether to restart massive attacks in an effort to bring the conflict to a close. "I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me." Why it matters: Though Trump has made similar threats before, his comments come ahead of a planned meeting Tuesday with leaders from six Gulf countries — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman — on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. The meeting could shape the next phase of the war, including whether to make another push for diplomacy or intensify military action. If Trump wants to resume major combat operations, he would need buy-in from his regional allies. The president has said several times in recent days that the war will end soon. Some U.S. officials warn that the conflict has settled into an unsustainable, neither-war-nor-peace stalemate, and they believe Trump could return to major combat operations after the midterms if a deal isn't reached by then. What he's saying: Trump made clear in the interview that he wants to use the meeting at the UN to hear directly from regional allies about the war's next steps. "I want to find out where they are and how they are doing. We have been very protective of them," Trump said. Trump declined to say whether he'll decide on the path forward before or after the midterms. Driving the news: In early August, Trump held off on resuming major combat operations after Saudi Arabia and Qatar expressed concern that Iran would bomb Saudi oil and gas facilities in retaliation. Since then, Trump has taken a "low-key" approach : suspending negotiations with Iran, launching a new economic sanctions campaign , continuing a naval blockade on Iranian ports, and focusing the U.S. military on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and increasing oil flow to the global energy…

33e1d7779a:47517343667e9e97.title: UN mission finds reasonable grounds to believe U.S. committed war crimes in Iran
33e1d7779a:47517343667e9e97.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:47517343667e9e97.summary: The U.S. may have committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran , including a mass-casualty strike on a school for which Washington has yet to claim responsibility, a UN fact-finding mission said Thursday. The big picture: The administration has waged a campaign of aggressive, norm-busting war-fighting, with the president repeatedly threatening to hit civilian infrastructure in his pressure campaign on Tehran. The president has shrugged off questions about his attacks on Iran and previously said he wasn't concerned if his threats could amount to war crimes. The White House and Pentagon did not immediately respond to Axios' request to respond to the UN team's findings. What's inside: The UN mission found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. carried out the Feb. 28 strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in southern Iran that reportedly killed more than 120 children. Back in May, U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper told the House Armed Services Committee the Minab attack "correlated" with a U.S. strike. And in June, President Trump said "nobody did that on purpose" and that "mistakes are made." The UN team found reasonable grounds to believe the U.S. carried out both the school strike and another on a sports center. Both, the UN report said, amount to war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack. CENTCOM has denied carrying out the sports center attack. What they're saying: The "U.S. failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective," the mission's report said of the school strike. The mission sought information on the strikes and attempted to meet with U.S. officials but received no response, the report said. Zoom out: The report further detailed "gross human rights violations" committed by Iran, including those that breached freedom from torture, fair trial and the right to freely assemble, among others. It said Iran has announced at least 58 executions since the start of 2026, including 29 men executed in…

33e1d7779a:98b2fa949a3b024f.title: States prep for ICE agents to be at polls, just in case
33e1d7779a:98b2fa949a3b024f.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:98b2fa949a3b024f.summary: The Trump administration's hints about sending ICE agents to election polling places this fall have led state officials from Maine to Oregon to make plans to counter any actions that could affect voters. Why it matters: It's illegal for federal law enforcement to be at polling places — and there are limits on how close local authorities can be — but when asked about ICE at the polls, President Trump said in May he'd "do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections." Earlier this month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE agents could be at polling places if they were serving an immigration warrant. "We would be engaging in malpractice if we didn't prepare for the concern [about ICE agents showing up at polls] and we didn't address it," New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver told Axios. The big picture: State election officials nationwide told Axios how they're working with local election officials and state attorneys general to prep for the possibility of ICE disrupting voting or ballot drop box operations. "ICE doesn't have a role here," said Aghogho Edevbie, Michigan's deputy secretary of state. "Certainly any ICE activity near a polling location can be considered voter intimidation, and we would take steps to counter that immediately." Zoom in: Toulouse Oliver said her office's preparations for any federal agents are similar to how it would deal with other unauthorized people at the polls. Her office is training local election officials to initially ask any officers to leave the voting area. If necessary, then they should call the county sheriff. The next step would be legal action against any unauthorized people. "An ICE agent is the same as any other unauthorized individual at a polling location, and the same protocols should be followed," she said. What they're saying: "If the Trump administration were to go down that path, the individuals involved would be committing crimes," Maine Secretary of State Shenna…

33e1d7779a:9c8f1f8c5cee6b3e.title: Hasan Piker on "The Axios Show": America worse than al-Qaeda "pound for pound"
33e1d7779a:9c8f1f8c5cee6b3e.author: Alex Thompson
33e1d7779a:9c8f1f8c5cee6b3e.summary: LOS ANGELES — Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker tells Axios he believes America conducts more terrorism in the world than al-Qaeda, the terror network that carried out the 9/11 attacks. "Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker said in an exclusive interview for a new episode of "The Axios Show." Piker added: "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world." Why it matters: Piker is one of the most popular streamers on Twitch, and his history of incendiary statements has become central to Republicans' attacks in the critical Senate race in Michigan since Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed had Piker campaign for him in the primary. Driving the news: Piker's comments to Axios came in response to a question about his previous statement that "America is the top dog in terrorism." Piker pointed to the deaths of more than 100 people at an elementary school in Minab, Iran, earlier this year. The AP found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school. "If you're killing 140 schoolgirls, that is an act of terror," he said. "This doesn't mean that all Americans are terrorists, but the reality of the matter is we have to create an environment of accountability to ensure things like that never happen again." The Trump administration has not yet released findings from a Pentagon investigation, and an exact death toll is not known. The big picture: Republican-affiliated groups already have spent nearly $3 million in ads attacking El-Sayed over his affiliation with Piker, according to the tracking firm AdImpact. Most of the ads feature a clip of Piker in 2019 saying that "America deserved 9/11." He apologized for the remark and has since argued that the terror attacks were part of "blowback" from U.S. involvement in the Middle East in previous decades. "This doesn't justify the action, mind you," he told Axios. "This is more so analysis to stop further violence from taking place, both violence in the region, but also violence in the home front…

33e1d7779a:086040a207bac687.title: AI's imminent hacking threat is hiding in plain sight
33e1d7779a:086040a207bac687.author: Bradley Olson
33e1d7779a:086040a207bac687.summary: An unprecedented wave of AI-powered, human-driven cyberattacks is coming, security experts say — and it's a far more urgent risk than theoretical conversations about AI wiping out humanity. Why it matters: The great September AI panic — which spread from boardrooms to Congress to American households in the last week — may have missed the point. Powerful models with advanced cybersecurity capabilities are already allowing attackers to bypass the human bottleneck that has long prevented most hacking campaigns from reaching industrial scale. Executives and former officials have told Axios they fear automated cyberattacks that turn off critical services like the power grid, or attackers using AI agents (like the ones that breached Hugging Face) to hack self-driving cars or create a botnet that takes over the whole internet. Driving the news: OpenAI on Wednesday disclosed six new incidents in which its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials, uploaded files to the public internet or communicated across supposedly isolated training environments. The big picture: Rather than seeing recent safety failures at OpenAI and other frontier labs as terrifying instances of agents running amok , seasoned cybersecurity experts instead say they represent cautionary tales illustrating what will happen when powerful models meet poor security controls. "The more we have been peeking under the hood to understand exactly what happened, the more we realize that there was a lot of human error in the picture," Michele Catasta, the president and head of AI at app builder Replit, told Axios. For the record : OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said the Hugging Face breach was the "first security incident that I have felt very viscerally," and the company has implemented new internal controls. Kai Chen, alignment research lead at OpenAI, told Axios in an interview Wednesday that the safety incidents they've faced are both due to internal systems and advancing model capabilities. "It's…

33e1d7779a:d300d402ff3248b2.title: Scoop: Trump to hold Iran talks with Gulf leaders next week
33e1d7779a:d300d402ff3248b2.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:d300d402ff3248b2.summary: President Trump is expected to hold a meeting with Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the war with Iran , three sources with direct knowledge tell Axios. Why it matters: The meeting is expected to focus on U.S. ideas for a postwar strategy as Trump and his senior team work on a day-after plan expected to be finalized after the midterms . What we're watching: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also wants to meet Trump in New York, but no meeting has been scheduled, an Israeli source said. Flashback: Last year, Trump met during the UN General Assembly with leaders from eight Arab and Muslim countries and presented them with his draft Gaza peace plan. He presented it publicly a week later. A deal to end the war was reached shortly afterward." Context: Gulf countries that host U.S. military bases suffered major Iranian attacks during the war as well as significant economic losses from disruptions to oil and natural gas exports." Driving the news: Trump said on Wednesday that "hopefully we are towards the end of the war. Trump claimed again that Iran wants to make a deal and said the U.S. heard it from Iran directly. State of play: The sources said Trump will meet with leaders or foreign ministers from the Gulf Cooperation Council countries — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. The White House declined to comment. What's next: The State Department sent out initial invitations on Wednesday. One of the sources said the meeting could expand to include other Arab and Muslim leaders.

33e1d7779a:c872da1c551416f5.title: Johnson-Massie feud boils over: "Why are we taking days off our calendar?"
33e1d7779a:c872da1c551416f5.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:c872da1c551416f5.summary: Mike Johnson 's decision to send the House home early — again — is fueling an increasingly bitter feud with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) over whether the speaker is using the calendar to dodge politically painful votes. Why it matters: The House will now be gone for more than six weeks ahead of the midterms, delaying Massie's effort to force a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the Iran war. "We had the Epstein recess last year. We got the Epstein recess this year, and then we got the Hegseth day off," Massie told Axios coming off an hourlong tirade on the House floor Wednesday. Massie's impeachment resolution has dim prospects in the GOP-controlled House, but it would have forced members to go on the record on Hegseth just weeks before the midterms. Driving the news: Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday as a privileged resolution, giving the House two legislative days to act. But Johnson's decision to cancel Thursday's session pushes the matter until after the election. "He cut off the day tomorrow to avoid the vote," Massie said. "The speaker could still have the vote today if he wanted. That's how we know he did this." Johnson (R-La.) disputed that characterization Wednesday, calling Massie's claim "ridiculous" and the Kentucky Republican's impeachment push a "publicity stunt." He said he expects the House to table the resolution when lawmakers return. Zoom in: It's not the first time Massie has accused Johnson of keeping the House out of session to avoid votes he is trying to force. Last year, Johnson kept the House out of session for nearly two months during the government shutdown, with Massie accusing the speaker of trying to stall his first discharge petition aimed at forcing release of government files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . Johnson also recently canceled the final two weeks of the September session — amid Massie's claim that he's closed in on the GOP…

33e1d7779a:ec55438bccc955e6.title: House votes to curb AI data center costs
33e1d7779a:ec55438bccc955e6.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:ec55438bccc955e6.summary: The House passed the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act on Wednesday, marking Congress' most significant step yet to shield consumers from the soaring infrastructure costs of the AI boom . Why it matters: Washington is facing growing pressure to put guardrails around AI's rapid expansion, from the technology itself to the data centers powering it. The bipartisan bill, which passed 417-3, would require state utility regulators to consider rules making data centers cover some of the costs of new power generation. Its passage gives lawmakers a tangible response to an issue that has quickly become a political flashpoint ahead of the midterms. Driving the news: The vote comes amid a broader reckoning over the pace and costs of AI development. Last weekend, leaders of some of the world's most powerful AI companies called for slowing the development of frontier AI models to give safety measures time to catch up. Data centers have become a focus of anti-AI sentiment, with 70% of Americans opposing construction in their area. Lawmakers in both parties have backed efforts to slow or restrict data center development amid concerns about electricity bills, strained power grids and water use. Catch up quick: The bill, led by Reps. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.) and Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), advanced out of the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July. GOP leadership had been previously non-committal about bringing it to the floor. The intrigue: The House's move comes as President Trump is arguing against pumping the brakes on AI development, framing U.S. dominance in the technology as a race against China. The only control or "guardrails" that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" the president posted Monday on Truth Social. Trump has also aggressively defended data center development amid growing local backlash, saying in an Aug. 31 Truth Social post that communities that reject the facilities will be "backwards and poor." "If they…

33e1d7779a:f6c1729bd8893a42.title: House passes Russia sanctions bill
33e1d7779a:f6c1729bd8893a42.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:f6c1729bd8893a42.summary: The House passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill Thursday, sending the long-awaited legislation to President Trump's desk. Why it matters: The measure would significantly expand economic pressure on Russia while handing Trump fresh authority to impose secondary tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian oil and gas. It would also target Russia's "shadow fleet," the network of aging tankers used to evade Western sanctions while exporting Russian oil. The vote was 262-159. The bill was renamed in honor of its lead sponsor, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who died suddenly in July. Driving the news: The bill scrambled the usual partisan lines on Russia and Ukraine, with House Democratic leaders opposing it while some rank-and-file Democrats backed the measure. Democratic leaders objected primarily over provisions handing Trump more tariff authority. Republicans rejected Democratic efforts in the Rules Committee earlier this week to strip the tariff authority or narrow how it could be used. Republicans in the isolationist wing of the party opposed the legislation amid broader resistance to further U.S. involvement in the Russia-Ukraine war. Catch up quick: The legislation has been more than a year in the making, dating back to a sanctions push Graham and dozens of senators launched in April 2025. The sanctions package has long had wide bipartisan support, but concerns from the White House held it up for months. Graham had been the key negotiator with the White House. The Senate passed the measure last month with broad bipartisan support after Trump officially backed the legislation.

33e1d7779a:119bef34f064d863.title: OpenAI discloses six new safety incidents
33e1d7779a:119bef34f064d863.author: Sam Sabin
