33e1d7779a:119bef34f064d863.summary: OpenAI on Wednesday disclosed six new incidents in which its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials, uploaded files to the public internet or communicated across supposedly isolated training environments. The company also announced a new procedure for reporting similar misbehavior in the future. Why it matters: It's increasingly clear that the Hugging Face breach wasn't a one-off incident, as AI models become more capable of finding unexpected ways to work around the guardrails meant to contain them. "There's currently no industry wide framework with explicit disclosure standards, so we're taking this step voluntarily because we think it's really important to share what we're learning," Kai Chen, research lead on the alignment team at OpenAI, told Axios. "We hope it really helps inform shared standards and regulations," Chen said. Zoom in: The six newly disclosed incidents ranged from models leaving instructions for their future selves to cover their tracks after cheating to using leaked API keys found on GitHub — with the earliest incident happening in October. An unreleased Astra-family model inserted jailbreak-like instructions into its own context summaries, including directions to ignore developer messages. OpenAI identified 27 affected summaries. During GPT-5.6 Sol training, models aimed to conceal mistakes, invent missing historical data and hide mismatches between source versions. A model searched public GitHub repositories for exposed API keys and attempted to use disposable email accounts before fabricating earnings data when it could not retrieve the requested information. Other examples: Models uploaded data and a task image to public file-hosting services on two occasions in October and January to obtain citations or external image-search results, without asking the user. Models used OpenAI's internal Artifactory repository as a message board to exchange requests and answers across separate training samples. Collaborating agents…

33e1d7779a:f321976142cbcbd0.title: Trump demands lower interest rates after Fed decision
33e1d7779a:f321976142cbcbd0.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:f321976142cbcbd0.summary: President Trump responded to the Federal Reserve raising interest rates for the first time in three years by saying they should be lowered — "AND FAST!" Why it matters: The rate hike immediately puts Trump at odds with the central bank under new Fed chair Kevin Warsh , whom he picked to lead it. By the numbers: The Fed raised its target interest rate by a quarter percentage point, to a range of 3.75%–4%. Fed projections show 12 of 18 officials expect one more rate hike this year, while four expect two more. What he's saying: " Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Our Country is BOOMING with new Investment! If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year," he added." "The word "Deficit" is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS. We are "carrying" almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" The intrigue: Trump didn't insult Warsh, though he often insulted his predecessor, Jerome Powell. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates.

33e1d7779a:e6d1bf088ce55cc1.title: U.S. diplomats meet with Houthis as Red Sea crisis intensifies
33e1d7779a:e6d1bf088ce55cc1.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:e6d1bf088ce55cc1.summary: American diplomats met over the weekend with Houthi representatives at the U.S. embassy in Oman and discussed tensions in the Red Sea, a regional source familiar with the issue confirmed. Why it matters: The meeting in Muscat, which was organized with the help of the Omani government, focused on maintaining a ceasefire between the U.S. and Houthis and guaranteeing that the Bab al-Mandeb Strait stays open, the source said. The U.S. is in a delicate position, wanting to keep a vital shipping lane open without getting drawn into Saudi Arabia's battle in Yemen against the Iran-backed Houthis. Washington has so far rejected Saudi requests to get involved militarily. The State Department declined to comment. Driving the news: The source said the U.S. was represented in the meeting by diplomats from the embassy, but the ambassador did not attend. The person added that Houthi representatives made clear during the meeting that they want the May 2025 ceasefire with the U.S. to continue. The source also said that Houthi representatives stressed their attacks were aimed only at Saudi ships as part of the renewed fighting between the two sides. They committed to allow freedom of navigation for all other ships through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. Reuters first reported on the meeting. What they're saying: On Monday, a day after the meeting, Vice President Vance told reporters that the U.S. is negotiating with the Houthis. "We've also been engaged in direct conversations with the Houthis themselves, so we actually feel like we are on top of the situation," he said. Between the lines: Secretary of State Rubio spoke on Tuesday with Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi and discussed the efforts for deescalation in the region, the State Department said. The call came after weeks of tensions between the U.S. and Oman. President Trump threatened to bomb Oman because of talks it had held with Iran about the Strait of Hormuz. State of play: The fighting between the Houthis and…

33e1d7779a:59ad0941f7d58bfb.title: Scoop: U.S. open to discuss AI "shared risks" with China, Bessent says
33e1d7779a:59ad0941f7d58bfb.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:59ad0941f7d58bfb.summary: The U.S. is open to discussing shared risks with China in upcoming AI talks this weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios. Why it matters: The Trump administration has flatly rejected calls from industry to pace or slow down the development of AI, citing a fierce race against China. Bessent's scheduled meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng could provide an opening for talks on U.S.-China AI safety cooperation. "The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems. We expect our discussions to cover both open and closed weight models," Bessent said in a statement to Axios. "Bessent and [United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer] are the point guys on China. So it makes sense the secretary is in this position," a senior administration official said. Driving the news: There will be multi-hour meetings in New York City, focused on AI, trade, rare earths, and other economic issues, building on previous discussions held in cities around the world, sources familiar said. The agenda will remain flexible to allow for substantive discussion across the range of relevant issues, sources added. Possible working-level meetings will continue into Monday, sources said. Catch up quick: Bessent has played a key role in the Trump administration's AI agenda. He was among the few cabinet members who flanked President Trump during a G7 press conference in June, where top AI CEOs and the administration discussed a U.S.-led effort to coordinate global AI standards. Bessent also helped cool Anthropic's relations with the administration following a fallout with the Pentagon and is viewed as a reasonable actor who is trusted by the private sector and critical infrastructure operators, sources familiar have previously told Axios. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick led high-profile AI discussions during the G20 summit in North Carolina earlier this month, while Bessent is taking…

33e1d7779a:95e4ef1e4685930d.title: AI environmental concerns build as lawmakers grapple with tech panic
33e1d7779a:95e4ef1e4685930d.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:95e4ef1e4685930d.summary: Data: The AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about the environmental impacts of AI, up more than ten percentage points from last year, per polling results out Wednesday. The big picture: It's just one area where Americans' AI concerns are building across the spectrum — highlighting one of the few issues lawmakers are crossing the aisle to confront amid ballooning panic set off by rogue models , industry warnings and public backlash . But it's unclear what, if any, role the AI backlash will play in the upcoming midterm elections, with voters split on who is better suited to handle the issue. Some Democratic lawmakers are reportedly hesitant to spend too much time discussing it on the campaign trail. President Trump has emerged as a top cheerleader for AI and the data centers needed to power the tech, with his administration moving to reshape environmental and permitting regulations for AI infrastructure. Driving the news: But that comes as 53% of Americans are extremely or very concerned about the environmental impacts of AI, according to a poll of 3,424 from The AP-NORC Center and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) conducted July 6 to 24. Democrats are more likely than Republicans to be extremely or very concerned at 65%, but 42% of Republicans shared that sentiment — a larger share than those who are somewhat concerned (26%) or not concerned at all (31%). Democrats are also more likely to say AI will be hurtful to society as a whole, per the polling , but half of Republicans are similarly pessimistic. Anxiety about data centers' impact on electricity prices, power outages or water supply is also wide-ranging, with roughly eight in 10 adults reporting being at least somewhat concerned about each. Zoom out: Separate polling out today found that a significant slice of Americans also…

33e1d7779a:2da6e3c51116a64a.title: Canada could become the EU's first "associate member"
33e1d7779a:2da6e3c51116a64a.author: Andrew Pantazi
33e1d7779a:2da6e3c51116a64a.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed making Canada the European Union's first "associate member." Why it matters: Canada and the EU are testing whether a nation deeply dependent on the U.S. market can find economic independence by moving closer to Europe. This could also present one of the most permanent effects of President Trump 's trade wars : U.S. allies building markets, supply chains and security ties designed to make them less vulnerable to Washington. If the proposal goes through, the shift would pull Ottawa deeper into Europe's economic and security architecture as Canada reduces its reliance on the U.S. — something Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has signaled the nation is open to . Driving the news: In her annual state of the union address, von der Leyen framed the Canada offer as part of Europe's response to a world where "old assumptions and relationships have frayed." Speaking directly to Carney, she said democracies "have the freedom to choose with whom to work." Her proposal would move beyond their existing trade pact to integrate their defense industries and deepen ties on manufacturing, technology, energy, and the Arctic. This comes after Trump has spent more than a year threatening Canada's economy and sovereignty , repeatedly calling for it to become the 51st state and imposing some of America's harshest tariffs. In addition to 50% tariffs, Trump will block certain Canadian dairy, alcohol and auto imports later this month. What they're not saying: The White House, the European Commission and the Canadian prime minister's office have not yet responded to requests for comment. Context: The EU already extends its single market without full membership to Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, but Canada's associate membership would likely differ. The single market guarantees the free movement of goods, services, capital and people, and it requires member states to accept Brussels' regulations. Canada already has…

33e1d7779a:64cf285e83857697.title: Exclusive: Warren backs pause on AI
33e1d7779a:64cf285e83857697.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:64cf285e83857697.summary: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is the latest prominent Democrat to back a pause on advanced artificial intelligence, her office told Axios exclusively. Why it matters: The idea of slowing down AI development — once considered a non-starter in a fierce race to beat China — is gaining momentum. Driving the news: Warren on Wednesday will call for a pause on advanced AI development but will stop short of calling for a ban on superintelligence, breaking with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). "We should immediately press pause on the development of advanced AI while lawmakers and regulators put systems in place to keep people safe," Warren will say ahead of a roundtable hosted by Sanders on Wednesday. "Congress must urgently pass legislation to put stronger guardrails in place before we have a cyberattack, economic crisis, or national security disaster facilitated by AI." Sanders' proposal calls for a pause and a ban on superintelligence, and threatens up to 20 years in prison for violations, which its authors note is similar to the penalties for illegally developing nuclear weapons. Between the lines: The progressive movement — like every other political faction — does not have a unified position when it comes to the nitty-gritty of AI regulation. Warren and Sanders have also released AI tax plans with varying approaches. Warren has proposed taxing AI companies, while Sanders wants the government to take equity stakes in them. Catch up quick: Frontier lab CEOs have coalesced around a message of pacing or slowing frontier AI development and seeking international collaboration. Warren said the industry's push to "pace the frontier" is "insufficient," arguing that elected officials, not AI CEOs, should decide the technology's future. Suggestions to weaken antitrust protections to confront AI risks are "transparently self-serving," she said. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for an exemption in antitrust law to help coordinate AI pacing. Former antitrust government…

33e1d7779a:10ec6ef92d042308.title: Exclusive: Kristen Silverberg named next president and CEO of Business Roundtable
33e1d7779a:10ec6ef92d042308.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:10ec6ef92d042308.summary: Kristen Silverberg, a widely respected policy expert and former ambassador, was named the new president and CEO of Business Roundtable , the top policy voice of America's leading CEOs. Silverberg, now BRT's president and chief operating officer, will succeed Josh Bolten , a former White House chief of staff who has led the organization for the past decade , when he steps down on Jan. 31. Why it matters: Business Roundtable is one of Washington's most influential associations. The 200+ members are CEOs of the biggest U.S.-based companies, most with global reach. The CEOs use BRT to amplify what they consider the most important messages business leaders can deliver to government. Silverberg — who worked with Bolten in the White House and is a former U.S. ambassador to the European Union from 2008 to 2009 — said in a statement that a key mission of BRT, American companies and their CEOs is championing and delivering growth and jobs. "The American economy is undergoing a profound transformation," she said. "Leaders in government and business have an extraordinary opportunity and a responsibility to strengthen American growth and competitiveness while expanding opportunity for workers and communities." "Business Roundtable has a critical role to play in advancing policies that make America the best place in the world to build, grow and invest in a business." The backstory: Silverberg, 55, was an assistant secretary of State under President George W. Bush and was a law clerk to Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas and Judge David Sentelle of the U.S. Court of Appeals. She's a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Texas School of Law. What they're saying: BRT chair Chuck Robbins, chair and CEO of Cisco Systems, called Silverberg a "proven and strategic leader, with the deep trust and respect of Business Roundtable's Board and members." "Kristen has been instrumental in positioning the organization and its leaders as effective advocates for policies that help…

33e1d7779a:cdb1df3ccd14c01d.title: An aging Congress attempts to regulate AI without using it
33e1d7779a:cdb1df3ccd14c01d.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:cdb1df3ccd14c01d.summary: Members of Congress and governors are under increasing pressure to regulate AI , but more than two dozen of them who spoke with Axios said they don't use the technology or have rarely done so. Why it matters: That striking admission — particularly among older, influential lawmakers — comes amid calls for an AI slowdown and warnings within the industry that it could end humanity if left unchecked. Critics argue that it's impossible for politicians to grasp how rapidly the technology is changing — and the threats or scientific breakthroughs it might unleash — if they don't use it or even dismiss it. One House Democrat called it "f*cking absurd," arguing, "Anyone who's overseeing this has to be someone who's a regular user." "That's a real problem," said Rob Flaherty, a 35-year-old Democratic digital strategist who co-founded a group to push his party to move faster in confronting AI. "Understanding what it can do is essential to figuring out what we ought to do about it." "As we begin to legislate on issues related to AI, it helps to have experience using it," said Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.), who's 47. Zoom in: Several lawmakers, including those steeped in seniority and in charge of key committees, told Axios they simply haven't tried AI. "Heavens no," said Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), 75, chair of the Armed Services Committee, when asked if he uses AI. "Personally? I don't think I've ever used it," said Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), 74, the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee. "No," Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai'i), 78, said when asked if she uses AI, but that "doesn't mean I won't." She added, "I don't think we in Congress have gotten quite our handle on what we should do and how much AI we should be regulating." "I do not personally use it," said Sen. James Risch (R-Idaho), 83, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair. On a personal level, "no," said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), 83. The House Appropriations Committee ranking member added that…

33e1d7779a:8bd0ff1b1777fc6e.title: Trump escalates war on federal data
33e1d7779a:8bd0ff1b1777fc6e.author: Mike Zapler
33e1d7779a:8bd0ff1b1777fc6e.summary: The nerdy, traditionally apolitical world of federal data is increasingly getting swept up in the Trump administration's push to control every level of government. Across the federal government, agencies are changing how they collect and publicize information. More and more, politics and ideology are part of the equation. Why it matters: Reliable, unbiased data informs nearly everything the federal government does — from distributing benefits and enforcing workplace discrimination laws to responding to public health threats. Driving the news: The administration's moves in recent weeks span an array of agencies and types of data. 🩺 Measles. Reuters reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked the CDC director to remove a reference to two deaths in Pennsylvania from its online tally of measles cases. The move came after the CDC had already accepted Pennsylvania officials' explanation that the deaths were linked to measles. Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro had spent days sparring on social media, each accusing the other of politicizing the deaths. Kennedy is a longtime vaccine skeptic. 🏡 Census Bureau. Last month, the Commerce Department did away with language barring political interference that had been part of the department's scientific integrity policy , NPR reported . The department oversees the Census Bureau and several other agencies. The move came after the bureau issued an unauthored report — promptly touted by President Trump — that found that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. The team behind the report, however, included officials with ties to the Trump-linked America First Institute . ⚠️ Anti-discrimination. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is planning to stop collecting data that's helped the agency investigate claims of workplace discrimination, The Guardian reported . For 60 years, the agency has examined the demographic makeup of company workforces to enforce anti-discrimination laws.…

33e1d7779a:1b36061db868906c.title: Household income hits record, but lower earners lose ground
33e1d7779a:1b36061db868906c.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:1b36061db868906c.summary: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, 1968 to 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplements ; Note: Census identifies breaks in the series in 2013 and 2017 due to methodological changes; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios U.S. household income hit a record in 2025, but the lowest earners barely shared in the gains, new Census data show. Why it matters: On paper, Americans look richer than ever. But broader measures of financial security show millions still getting squeezed by medical costs , uneven income gains and a thinning public safety net. The 2025 Census report largely captures the economy before the major safety-net reductions in President Trump's " Big Beautiful Bill" took hold. That makes this year's record income and near-record-low official poverty numbers an important benchmark for measuring what happens next. By the numbers: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, the highest inflation-adjusted level since Census records began in 1967. Median post-tax household income climbed 3.1% to $76,060. The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year, dropping slightly to 10.2%, or about 34.5 million people. Child poverty fell to a record-low 13.4%, while poverty among Hispanics dropped to an unprecedented 13.9%. State of play: The economy delivered historic topline numbers without spreading the gains evenly. Income among the wealthiest 10% of Americans rose 1.7%, while income among the bottom 10% showed no significant change — indicating that the low-income households largely missed out on the gains. Households at the 90th percentile earned about $261,300, more than 13 times the roughly $20,010 earned at the 10th percentile. The top fifth of households captured 52.4% of all household income. The bottom fifth reported earning just 3%. Zoom in: Latinos offer one of the clearest examples of the split-screen economy in 2025. Hispanic poverty fell to its lowest level since Census began tracking it in 1973. But the median…

33e1d7779a:7df50aa57021ec43.title: Tech giants launch flexible-power coalition for data centers
33e1d7779a:7df50aa57021ec43.author: Amy Harder
33e1d7779a:7df50aa57021ec43.summary: A new coalition launched Wednesday is seeking a triple win for a data center industry that lately has struggled to notch any wins at all. The big picture: Tech giants Google and Nvidia are partnering with startup Emerald AI to back data centers that can flex their power demand — a strategy they say could curb electricity prices, mollify angry neighbors and grow the economy with more AI infrastructure. The launch comes amid mounting backlash to data centers centered on their resource impacts and power prices, and new polling shows the public-opinion challenge is getting steeper. What they're saying: "It's really a win-win-win solution," said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at Nvidia, in a call with reporters Monday ahead of the official launch of the coalition, called the AI Energy Management Alliance . State of play: The coalition brings together 20 companies and organizations spanning the AI and energy sectors, including Anthropic, utilities National Grid and AES, and power producers Constellation, NRG and RWE. The group is technically a relaunch. An earlier iteration, the Advanced Energy Management Alliance, was founded in 2014 to advocate for demand-response companies but had become largely inactive, Emerald AI CEO Varun Sivaram said on Monday's call. The revamped group is narrowly focused on making AI data centers more flexible power users — and convincing regulators and utilities to reward them for it. Friction point: A whopping 84% of Americans say they're concerned about data centers' impact on local electricity prices, according to new AP-NORC/University of Chicago Energy Policy Institute polling released Wednesday . More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about AI's environmental impacts, up from 41% a year ago. In a rare point of bipartisan agreement, roughly equal shares of Democrats and Republicans — 79% and 76%, respectively — support requiring data center developers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to support them. How it…

33e1d7779a:1883a06fccf0b059.title: Girls flag football is fastest-growing high school sport
33e1d7779a:1883a06fccf0b059.author: Brad Jennings
33e1d7779a:1883a06fccf0b059.summary: Data: NFHS ; Map: Brad Jennings/Axios Girls flag football has become the fastest-growing high school sport, as tens of thousands take up a game that barely had a varsity footprint a few years ago. Why it matters: Few girls high school sports have moved from niche to mainstream so quickly, broadening athletic opportunities in the process. By the numbers: More than 102,000 girls played high school flag football in 2025-26, a 551% increase in the past four years, according to the National Federation of State High School Associations . Catch up quick: In 2024, just 12 states sanctioned high school girls flag football, viewed as a safer, more accessible version of America's most popular spectator sport. Today, 23 states plus Washington, D.C., sanction it as an official varsity sport , and 3,990 schools reported participants in 2025-26. The NFL is backing its growth, too. It has invested millions to launch and expand high school programs , and featured the sport in its Super Bowl commercials . Beyond high schools, flag football will debut at the 2028 Olympics, and at least 40 NCAA schools already offer it as a collegiate varsity sport. Reality check: It's not yet clear whether flag football is mostly creating new high school athletes or pulling girls from established sports. A recent Newsday analysis on Long Island found flag participation rising sharply while girls lacrosse, softball and track participation fell. What we're watching: Girls varsity wrestling is undergoing its own boom. All 50 states now report girls wrestling participation, and 40 state athletic associations hold girls wrestling championships, up from just five about a decade ago.

33e1d7779a:d97879045963f423.title: AI panic sparks rare bipartisan moment on Capitol Hill
33e1d7779a:d97879045963f423.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:d97879045963f423.summary: Lawmakers who want to regulate AI are doing something unusual as Congress barrels towards a lengthy recess with no tangible solution in sight: They're working across the aisle. Why it matters: Bipartisanship is increasingly elusive on Capitol Hill of late, but it remains a crucial first step for action in a Senate that requires 60 votes to pass most legislation. The latest example: Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) are pressing congressional leadership for a vote on their bill to establish a federal program to assess and monitor AI systems. "Recent incidents of rogue AI agent swarms hacking into public websites and systems have removed lingering doubts concerning the ability of these agents to wreak havoc on our cyber infrastructure," the pair wrote in a letter first obtained by Axios. "Congress cannot delay legislating to address frontier AI risks much longer. Industry-led evaluations are not enough." State of play: Several new bipartisan efforts to regulate AI have cropped up in the week since several current and former employees at Anthropic and OpenAI went public with concerns about the existential risks posed by their own products. Reps. Russell Fry (R-S.C.) and Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) are founding a caucus focused on AI small businesses, called the Innovators Caucus, as Axios first reported Monday. Among the group's stated goals is starting work on a federal framework to regulate AI, as well as bringing small businesses to the AI policymaking table. The doomsday warnings have also breathed new life into existing bipartisan proposals to mitigate the dangers of AI. Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) has been publicly hawking his bill with Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) to require AI companies to include a human-activated "kill switch" in their systems. Lieu has also privately pitched Democratic leadership on creating a bipartisan AI select committee if they retake control of the House next year. Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte…

33e1d7779a:79527d1b5cb6fb24.title: Rep. Chuck Edwards files complaint against House Ethics
33e1d7779a:79527d1b5cb6fb24.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:79527d1b5cb6fb24.summary: Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) filed a complaint against the top Republican and Democrat on the House Ethics Committee on Tuesday, accusing the lawmakers who investigated him of breaking their own rules. Why it matters: Edwards is escalating his fight against the committee just two weeks after the House voted 413-2 to censure him over its findings that he violated House rules related to sexual harassment and a hostile workplace. Edwards' complaint asks the Office of Congressional Conduct to investigate Ethics Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) over their handling of his case. The Ethics Committee has previously disputed Edwards' account of the process. When it released its report last month, Guest and DeSaulnier said Edwards had agreed to waive certain procedural steps after reviewing a draft of the report several days earlier. The committee's findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate. Driving the news: "There was nothing ethical about this process," Edwards said in announcing the complaint. He alleges the committee circumvented its own rules by adopting its final report and recommending his censure before receiving his formal response. Edwards has maintained that his conduct did not violate House rules, though he did apologize to his wife, family, and the two women he allegedly harassed. The committee declined to comment. Catch up quick: The Ethics report's findings corroborated several anecdotes previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings. He told one staffer that she had "written a complex chapter in my heart" shortly before she was set to leave his office in a three-page handwritten letter previously reported by Axios. Edwards gave the two young female staffers numerous…

33e1d7779a:924e2bb08fb3511d.title: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back
33e1d7779a:924e2bb08fb3511d.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:924e2bb08fb3511d.summary: The Epstein files fight that consumed the House last year is threatening to engulf Republicans all over again. Why it matters: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is now just one Republican away from having the support he needs to force another politically painful Epstein vote — and he and his allies are hunting for the final GOP signature. Retiring Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) signed Massie's new discharge petition Monday, joining Massie and Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.). Massie and Mace told Axios they're actively targeting retiring Republicans and members in vulnerable districts for the fourth GOP signature that will get them the magic number to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), one of four Republicans who bucked President Trump and GOP leadership to sign Massie's first Epstein petition last year, told Axios she's considering signing again and has been having conversations with Massie. The big picture: The push is reviving one of the most disruptive fights of Trump's second term for House Republicans. Last year's Epstein discharge petition became a months-long headache for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and the White House before ultimately securing 218 signatures and forcing the issue onto the House floor. The bill passed with almost unanimous support in the House. The Epstein Files Transparency Act II would enforce and expand the release of remaining files at DOJ. "The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public. In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing," Massie wrote in a s tatement last month . Reality check: Even if Massie locks down the Republican support he needs this week, the House is set to leave Washington Thursday until after the November midterms, meaning any potential floor showdown would come post-election. Democrats also still need to provide the remaining signatures needed to reach…

33e1d7779a:58f465c242ebaf0b.title: How Ed Sheeran's tour imploded over a geopolitical fight
33e1d7779a:58f465c242ebaf0b.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:58f465c242ebaf0b.summary: Ed Sheeran's world tour spiraled into chaos this week after one opener was removed, every remaining opening act quit and stadiums threatened to pull the plug on the tour. Why it matters: The turmoil reveals the power dynamics behind major concert tours, showing how even a global star like Sheeran can be forced to take a back seat on decisions about his own shows. Driving the news: All four of Sheeran's remaining supporting acts announced Tuesday that they were dropping out. Irish musicians Aaron Rowe and Beoga , as well as Danish band Lukas Graham , said Tuesday they were leaving the tour. Rowe was set to replace Macklemore as the opener for the U.S. shows, AP reports. Finneas, who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, also announced he was exiting the concert series, saying on Instagram that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed." Catch up quick: The moves came one day after rapper Macklemore, who was scheduled for most of the remaining tour dates, was dropped after using his sets to voice support for Palestinians and condemn the war in Gaza during shows on Sept. 4-5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Macklemore told the MetLife crowd on Sept. 4 that he wanted to do the tour so he could "say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'" His performance included images of war-torn Gaza playing on the video board. The tour's promoters, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone Monday that concert venues threatened to cancel shows unless Macklemore was dropped from the tour after his pro-Palestinian comments. Zoom in: Macklemore said the decision came after he spoke with Sheeran, alleging that the headliner faced pressure from stadium owners including Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium. According to Macklemore, Sheeran is typically "apolitical" and the recent round of backlash "challenged" him "in a way it never had before." The other side: Sheeran shared…

33e1d7779a:33c41e5ebe09157a.title: House quashes another Trump impeachment push with Dem help
33e1d7779a:33c41e5ebe09157a.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:33c41e5ebe09157a.summary: The House voted for the third time in two years to quash a rogue effort by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to impeach President Trump. Why it matters: As with the last two times, the vote divided House Democrats. Some sided with Green, but others voted "present" or actively helped GOP leadership defeat the effort. Green frustrated his Democratic colleagues by forcing the vote without support from party leadership, with one telling Axios the move was "fucked up." The Texas Democrat defended his attempts to impeach Trump over killings committed by federal immigration officials, calling it a "life and death" matter. Driving the news: The House voted 232-147 for Republican leadership's measure to table — effectively, kill — Green's motion to force a vote on impeaching Trump, with 47 members voting "present." Between the lines: Some Democrats who voted with Green privately sneered before the vote that it was a distraction from party messaging on the House's last in-session week before the midterm. Green pushed back by saying the lawmakers who criticized him "don't have the courage to stand up and face me" and challenging them to debate the matter publicly.

33e1d7779a:203cabe0ec4e2624.title: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building
33e1d7779a:203cabe0ec4e2624.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:203cabe0ec4e2624.summary: The Kennedy Center's board voted Tuesday to close the iconic performing arts center's main building for a renovation project championed by President Trump , multiple outlets reported and a source familiar confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Trump's attempts to put his name on the building , which memorializes former President John F. Kennedy, have fueled an ongoing legal and political battle. The decision came hours after a federal judge again said the center could not put Trump's name on the building . Driving the news: Axios could not immediately confirm when the closure will happen or how long it will be. A resolution from the board, filed as evidence in the ongoing legal fight with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over the Center, listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. The resolution cited "water intrusion and deterioration of the center's physical plant" that it said "caused a partial ceiling collapse," arguing the safety risk "greatly outweighs any reputational risk associated with closing the main building." Zoom out: A second resolution filed on Monday listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. The resolution states that without his name on the building, it's "unlikely" Trump "will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building." It listed options for text on the exterior marble beneath the center's name, including "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" or "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump." Friction point: U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper blocked the center from closing earlier this year, finding that "the Board was derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" and "based its decision on an insufficient, one-sided…

33e1d7779a:75b68fe3d9121b02.title: Scoop: Trump pollster gives GOP a data center survival guide
33e1d7779a:75b68fe3d9121b02.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:75b68fe3d9121b02.summary: President Trump's longtime pollster is offering Republican candidates a detailed playbook for neutralizing Democratic attacks over AI data centers — down to what language they should and shouldn't use. Why it matters: Republican strategists say GOP candidates have been all over the map in responding to the backlash to data centers. The goal is to put Republicans on offense after months of playing defense on the issue. Driving the news: Pollster Tony Fabrizio warns in a two-page memo obtained by Axios that "unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position." Fabrizio specifically advises candidates not to say, "I support building more data centers," warning: "It will be clipped and show up in ads." Instead, he tells Republicans to support AI infrastructure only if developers pay for their own power needs, protect consumers from higher utility bills and safeguard local water and natural resources. Fabrizio argues that candidates must make clear those conditions are enforceable, rather than voluntary commitments from tech companies. "This converts the candidate from a defender of technology companies into the person imposing rules on them," Fabrizio writes in the memo, which was sent Monday. Fabrizio offers a three-step script for candidates. First, "validate" voters' concerns about higher utility bills, the power grid and water use. Second, "draw the line" by vowing not to support projects that force families to subsidize them or allow tech companies to harm surrounding communities. Finally, argue that projects should move forward only if companies provide their own power, protect ratepayers and safeguard local water. "The order matters," Fabrizio writes. "It adopts voters' concerns as the approval standard instead of asking them to set those concerns aside." Fabrizio warns against generic support for "more data centers," leading with jobs or China, dismissing local concerns or defending individual projects before their costs and resource…

33e1d7779a:07ceef7f54def9b4.title: Trump considered dangerous, corrupt by majority in new poll
33e1d7779a:07ceef7f54def9b4.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:07ceef7f54def9b4.summary: Data: The Economist/YouGov ; Chart: Avery Lotz A slight majority of registered voters describe President Trump as corrupt and dangerous, a recent poll found, while just 14% say he isn't divisive. The big picture: Simply put, polling hasn't been pretty for the president — or for his Iran war , tariffs or other top priorities . Still, with the midterms weeks away, Trump has centered himself, making the election a referendum on his presidency . By the numbers: " Corrupt" (53%) and "dangerous" (51%) led the list of descriptors voters applied to Trump in the Sept. 11-14 The Economist-YouGov poll of 1,461 U.S. registered voters. Those words were followed by "out-of-touch" (47%), "cruel" (46%) and "bold" (45%). Just 18% said they'd use the word "steady" to describe the president. Worth noting: Democrats are testing an anti-corruption midterm message as Americans' perceptions of government corruption hit a 20-year high , per Gallup's trend , and polls show Americans believe the president has inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency while in office. The results broke sharply by party — 91% of Democrats and 62% of independents said Trump was corrupt, compared with 10% of Republicans. Republicans weren't universally positive: Less than half (49%) said they'd use the word "honest" to describe the president. Just 10% said it didn't describe him, while 41% had no opinion. Similarly, 38% of Republicans said he was steady, while 53% said they had no opinion. What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars." Ingle also accused Democrats in Congress of failing to stop waste, fraud and abuse in government. Zoom out: Trump's approval rating ticked up from the lowest point of his political career, recorded last month in Reuters-Ipsos' trend , this month. Some 35% of Americans…

33e1d7779a:8937b2505ec704e8.title: Massie moves to impeach Pete Hegseth over Iran War
33e1d7779a:8937b2505ec704e8.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:8937b2505ec704e8.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , accusing him of defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran. Why it matters: The impeachment effort is a long shot in the GOP-controlled Congress, but Massie's resolution is privileged, meaning he can force a full House vote and put Republicans on the record over Hegseth's handling of the Iran war. It's a dramatic escalation in the retiring lawmaker's months-long push to rein in the Trump administration's war powers. The effort also comes after the House has repeatedly voted on efforts to constrain the administration's military campaign in Iran, including passing war powers resolutions in June and July directing the president to end U.S. hostilities with Tehran. The House is slated to vote Tuesday on another war powers resolution on the Iran war effort. Driving the news: Massie's resolution accuses Hegseth of carrying out orders to continue operations in Iran despite Congress' constitutional authority over war and its votes seeking to end the conflict. Massie argued Hegseth's actions "frustrated Congress's ability to exercise its most solemn constitutional responsibility" and allowed an "unlawful war" to continue. "In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense," Massie said on the House floor. The eight-article resolution also targets Hegseth over U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, including accusing him of illegally directing the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization. Zoom out: Hegseth already faced a separate impeachment push from House Democrats, who introduced six articles against him in April that included allegations he waged an unauthorized war against Iran. What's next: The House will have to take up the legislation within the next two legislative days, but GOP leaders could also move to vote on tabling the…

33e1d7779a:3edb7a6d47983688.title: Kennedy Center's attempt to put Trump's name on building blocked again by judge
33e1d7779a:3edb7a6d47983688.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:3edb7a6d47983688.summary: A federal judge ruled Tuesday that the Kennedy Center's latest attempt to put President Trump's name on the performing arts center violated his earlier order blocking its renaming . The big picture: The order came just before the Kennedy Center's board, now composed of Trump loyalists, is set to weigh shutting down the building for renovations that members argue must include Trump being "appropriately recognized" on the structure. Driving the news: While Trump allies have argued the latest attempt to recognize Trump does not violate the law, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper said "[l]inguistic gymnastics cannot extricate the Kennedy Center's Board from an operative judicial order or the governing statute it was designed to enforce." Cooper ordered for Trump's name to be removed from the building in May, saying only Congress could change the name of the center that memorializes President John F. Kennedy. The judge blocked the center from putting an inscription that read "renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump" on the main building or renaming the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." Cooper wrote, "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing." This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:331d4536f995c29f.title: Trump turns on the Supreme Court he helped build
33e1d7779a:331d4536f995c29f.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:331d4536f995c29f.summary: President Trump lashed out at the Supreme Court on Tuesday after it struck down the president's mail-in voting order Monday night. Why it matters: The president slammed the justices over rulings they've issued against him this year, suggesting without evidence that the three justices he appointed to the court are being controlled by the left. What they're saying: "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "[T]hey are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won't be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal. "It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country's history." "It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court - it will likely cost me dearly for years to come - but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!" Zoom in: Trump unloaded on the court for striking down his birthright citizenship policy, in which the justices upheld that those born on American soil are citizens. He also slammed their "horrible decision on Tariffs ," after they ruled those unlawful earlier this year. "Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America," Trump wrote. Between the lines: Without naming them, Trump criticized the three justices he appointed: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. He explicitly praised Justices Alito and Thomas, who dissented in Monday's mail-in ballot ruling. The Supreme Court could not be immediately reached for comment. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:303f5598226c0bf6.title: Cities challenge Trump immigration rule over public benefits access
33e1d7779a:303f5598226c0bf6.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:303f5598226c0bf6.summary: New York City and five other Democratic-led local governments sued the Department of Homeland Security to block a new Trump administration rule they say will drive immigrants and mixed-status families away from public benefits they can legally receive. Why it matters: The cities warn the rule could drive hundreds of thousands out of health, food and housing programs , worsening public health , increasing homelessness and shifting millions of dollars in costs to local hospitals and governments. "… The data is clear: denying people services does not erase their need; it compounds it, generating a greater cost to our system that will be placed on the backs of working people for years to come. Nothing about this rule will reduce waste or keep Americans safer or improve New Yorkers' lives. It is simply a vehicle for confusion and a vehicle for cruelty." Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, told Axios that "[e]xtreme Democrats are once again fighting to give benefits to illegal aliens at the expense of American taxpayers. Immigrants must be able to…

33e1d7779a:eaa87cd3584cdb32.title: Scoop: U.S. attacked Iranian boats trying to seize Navy drone
33e1d7779a:eaa87cd3584cdb32.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:eaa87cd3584cdb32.summary: The U.S. military destroyed two Iranian small boats Monday after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps tried to steal a Navy drone patrolling the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The unusual incident shows how efforts to restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continues direct confrontation with Iran . The U.S. military initially didn't disclose the strike, and Iranian media presented it as a drone strike on "fishing boats." Driving the news: According to Iranian media , two fishing boats were struck Monday off the coast of the port city of Kargan and near Larak Island in Hormozgan province. Ahmad Nafisi, the province's deputy governor for security affairs, attributed the strike to the U.S. military. Nafisi said an unspecified number of fishermen were missing and that search-and-rescue operations were underway, according to Iran's semi-official Mehr News Agency. Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the IRGC used the boats to try to capture a naval drone that the U.S. military uses to patrol the Strait of Hormuz. After U.S. forces identified the attempt, an American drone fired two missiles at the boats, destroying them and killing most of those on board. What they are saying: U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the attempted seizure, saying "Iranian small boats recently attempted to take possession of a U.S. unmanned surface vessel, but they were unsuccessful after CENTCOM forcefully responded." "The surface drone remains under U.S. operational control," Hawkins said. State of play: The incident took place as the U.S. attempts to protect increased commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil flows remain below prewar levels. A U.S. official said the U.S. military and Gulf countries have begun conducting daytime transits of tankers through the strait and not only night time as was the case in recent month. As fighting with the Houthis in the Red Sea escalates, Saudi Arabia has…

33e1d7779a:5011ce21f4a8cd57.title: House Democrats face divisions on Russian sanctions bill
33e1d7779a:5011ce21f4a8cd57.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:5011ce21f4a8cd57.summary: House Democratic leadership is vocally opposing a Russia sanctions bill set to come to a vote this week, but not all of their members are comfortable taking that stance just yet. Why it matters: Republicans will reportedly need some Democratic votes to make up for defections from their isolationist wing and pass the measure. At issue for many Democrats is that the bill, named in honor of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), would allow the Trump administration to impose up to 100% tariffs on the five top importers of Russian oil. That has forced Democrats to choose between two issues that have become shibboleths for their party: support for Ukraine and opposition to giving President Trump more power to set trade policy. State of play: Reps. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and Richard Neal (D-Mass.) — the ranking members of the House Foreign Affairs, Joint Economic and Ways & Means committees, respectively — announced their opposition to the bill in a joint statement last week. "House Democrats are rock solid in our support for Ukraine, but the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia And Iran Act would do more harm than good," they said. "This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable." Yes, but: Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), an arch-centrist who often breaks with party leadership, told Axios last week he is "almost certainly going to be a 'yes' on the bill. "I think the sanctions [are good] but I am also generally supportive of tariffs," said Golden. The Maine Democrat has been his party's lone cheerleader for many of Trump's more controversial protectionist trade measures. Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) , the co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus, told Axios she is "reviewing [the bill] very carefully" and "working with our Ukraine Caucus." "I think it's important to send Russia a message that she needs to stand down," Kaptur added. Rep. Mike…

33e1d7779a:be7129a6dc7b6f71.title: Scoop: Top House Democrat launches investigation into Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding
33e1d7779a:be7129a6dc7b6f71.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:be7129a6dc7b6f71.summary: The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is investigating a Russian oligarch's reported financial involvement in a celebration related to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding , Axios has learned. Why it matters: Garcia is poised to be Congress' lead investigator if Democrats retake the House. This probe offers a pretty good hint of the direction he'll go in that role. "Oversight Democrats are investigating the numerous ways in which the Trump family have sought to enrich themselves on the basis of their proximity to President Donald Trump," Garcia stated in a letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. In a separate letter to Trump Jr. , Garcia wrote that ProPublica's reporting on Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev's role in funding the event "may be the most serious allegation against you to date." Driving the news: Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, provided hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of expenses for the May party in the Bahamas, according to ProPublica. Kremlev is close to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and his boxing organization is financed by Russian state-owned energy company Gazprom. The oligarch paid for one of the two private islands where the event was held and a fireworks show, according to ProPublica, despite Trump Jr.'s estimated $300 million net worth . A Trump Jr. spokesperson did not dispute the payments to ProPublica, telling the outlet Kremlev is "a personal friend of Don," but "not someone he has a business relationship with." Kremlev's press office told ProPublica the two met "a couple of years ago" and "have a friendly relationship," and that he has "never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances." Trump Jr.'s wife, Bettina Anderson, said in a statement on Instagram that it is "unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister," adding, "Friendship doesn't require a political motive." President Trump said in a…

33e1d7779a:3e5d5e16d0e7f882.title: Baal out: Top diplomat's worry about pagan god elicits eye rolls
33e1d7779a:3e5d5e16d0e7f882.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:3e5d5e16d0e7f882.summary: The second-most powerful man at the State Department put the brakes on a U.S. international exhibit featuring a bull statue because he worried it might look like Baal, a pagan god some associate with Satanic child sacrifice. Why it matters: The anecdote illustrates the quirky interests of Deputy Secretary of State Chris Landau, according to department critics, who say he spends too much time on social media focusing on the unimportant. Zoom in: The issue revolves around an international exposition next year in Belgrade, Serbia , where the U.S. plans to feature a statue of a bucking bull at an exhibit celebrating the American West. On Aug. 19, at 4:15 p.m., Landau sent an email to staffers about it: "I remain somewhat concerned by the Golden Bull imagery! Did a quick internet search and don't want it to become a distraction. The golden calf from the Bible is often portrayed as a golden bull." Providing hyperlinked footnotes and images of golden bull worship, Landau explored the ancient history of Baal as well as the "Modern Cultural Comparisons." "The imagery of a golden bull or calf is frequently invoked metaphorically today," he wrote. "For instance, critics and commentators sometimes compare modern financial fixations—typified by the famous Charging Bull statue on Wall Street to the ancient worship of material idols." Behind the scenes: The email, which was forwarded to multiple officials, elicited eyerolls and snickers inside the State Department. The bull statue was put on hold as State officials spent the last few weeks debating how to make it both interesting and non-Satanic. "It's just totally weird stuff and it's really indicative of the guy," a State Department official said. "Literally, no one thinks about Baal unless they're spending way too much time online, which Landau is," a different U.S. official lamented. "It's like an episode of Veep. Someone should tell him this is a Western bull, not a Near East bull," a third U.S. official said. Landau…

33e1d7779a:0de26086624a840f.author: Bradley Olson
33e1d7779a:0de26086624a840f.summary: Most agree the AI industry needs oversight. The critical barrier: Few really trust the industry, or the safety advocates who come from inside the house. Why it matters: Factions in the Trump administration, business executives wary of competitive threats, and advocates for cheaper, more customizable "open" models fear that new regulatory hurdles will offer frontier AI companies too much power. What they're saying: "I do not want a few humans in control of intelligence," Gavin Baker, a top tech investor and commentator on the AI race, said Sunday on X . Baker said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was surely sincere when he proposed new AI regulatory proposals in an essay Saturday , although the moves "would be good for his business over the long-term." Catch up quick : Four leading U.S. AI companies endorsed a potential pause in AI development this weekend after a series of troubling hacking incidents and awe-inducing displays of new model capabilities. The suggested pause caused a dip in global markets Monday as investors pondered what a slowdown in AI, one of the few reliable engines of economic growth this year, would do to economies around the world. Any hope of quick action extending from that fragile unity quickly shattered as critics spoke up and made clear just how much they distrust frontier AI players. AI distrust, explained Here are the key factors shaping that distrust, which are poised to delay the kind of "all-hands-on-deck" response many want. 💰Money : Anthropic stands alone in the history of capitalism, a company whose leaders are so concerned with safety that it broke away from OpenAI. Its employees, up to the CEO, honestly believe its product is so dangerous that there's a chance it could destroy humanity. And yet, as soon as this week, it's expected to file for what many expect will be the biggest IPO of all time, seeking to raise $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation. 33e1d7779a:04e1eda56ffb33a1.title: "I am the Hoax Buster": Trump's war on AI doomers gets personal
33e1d7779a:04e1eda56ffb33a1.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:04e1eda56ffb33a1.summary: President Trump declared war on the AI safety panic Monday, dismissing the industry's apocalyptic warnings as part of a "sick conspiracy" to sabotage America and his legacy. Why it matters: Trump is rewriting a complex, years-long debate over AI's dangers in the partisan grammar that has defined MAGA for a decade — hoaxes, conspiracies, traitors and, at the center of it all, one man. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT," Trump wrote in a barrage of pro-AI Truth Social posts, where he accused Democrats of stoking the panic. State of play: Monday marked a sharp escalation in the administration's long-standing opposition to AI regulation, as Trump recast the safety debate in starkly personal terms. Trump explicitly placed AI doomerism in the same bucket as the Russia investigation , climate change and his impeachments — the latest entry in a catalog of "hoaxes" that has also included the Epstein files and the affordability crisis . He turned his fire on the AI leaders urging restraint, questioning why CEOs would seek regulations that could cripple their own companies and arguing that any slowdown would squander America's lead over China. The intrigue: Trump's campaign against AI doomerism then spilled onto the stage of the "All In Summit" in Los Angeles, where Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a call from the president in the middle of a live interview. Addressing thousands of tech executives, investors and founders on speakerphone, Trump dismissed fears of an AI takeover as a "hoax" and assured the crowd that "the robots will not be taking over." Screenshot via Truth Social Between the lines: Trump is grafting his own political grievances onto a counter-narrative already taking hold among his Silicon Valley allies: that the AI panic is manufactured. David Sacks, Trump's influential AI adviser and "All In" podcaster, has portrayed AI alarmism as the work of a well-funded " Doomer Industrial Complex " that includes…

33e1d7779a:6f5d7e6301e925f6.title: Supreme Court strikes down USPS mail-in voting rule
33e1d7779a:6f5d7e6301e925f6.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:6f5d7e6301e925f6.summary: The Supreme Court struck down the U.S. Postal Service's rule restructuring mail-in voting Monday, halting a major Trump administration priority. The big picture: The 7-2 decision is a major win for voting rights advocates and the states that challenged the administration's plan; it also reverses the Supreme Court's earlier green light for President Trump's mail-in voting order. The justices' prior unsigned order allowing the rule to proceed was not a ruling on the merits — but this time around, they decided the government is "unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge." The rule would require states to submit lists of eligible voters to USPS, and the agency would then verify that those voters were receiving mail-in ballots before sending them out. The rule also had strict requirements on envelope design. Driving the news: While the court rejected the administration's stance, at least one concurring justice disagreed on the merits of the case. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion with fellow Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority" but that applying the proposed rules would be "arbitrary and capricious" for the midterm elections as state and local officials "do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule." Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented in a separate opinion. In their opinion, they called the filings claiming harm by some plaintiffs "cryptic" and that the USPS has the authority to implement a rule because Congress has empowered it to do so. Zoom out: The decision is likely the final say on the rule during this election cycle, with even U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani saying from the bench earlier this month that it was unclear how the government would implement the plans with November just around the corner. Steven Monteith, executive vice president at the Postal Service, said in a declaration…

33e1d7779a:0553244f5e7be04e.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:0553244f5e7be04e.summary: Majority Leader John Thune is asserting Congress' prerogative to act on AI — but he's urging a "light touch" even in the face of "consequential risks." Why it matters: On his first day back after a five-week break, Thune (R-S.D.) outlined his vision for congressional action on an issue President Trump has dismissed as a " hoax ." "Congress has a job to do," Thune said. "I think there are some potential consequential risks associated with AI," Thune told reporters when asked if he believes AI poses an existential threat to humanity. He added, "Guardrails there make sense to me" about cutting-edge, frontier AI models. But Thune also said that "there are always people who are creating a worst-case-scenario-type conversation out there." Driving the news: An AI panic is rippling through Congress, but mostly on the Democratic side, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) calling to "slow down the pace of development" of AI to avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome. Publicly, Trump is professing not to be concerned and insists that he should have the sole authority to regulate AI. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he posted on his Truth Social account Monday morning. Zoom out: Republicans aren't questioning Trump's ability to lead the country's approach to AI regulation, but they are suggesting that Congress has a role to play. And they aren't ruling out legislation. "So we may need to do something," Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said. "But there are existing guardrails, and corporate responsibility is a big part of this." Zoom in: Thune said he spoke with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) on Saturday night about their AI bill, which would force companies creating frontier AI models to guard against catastrophic risks and submit to federal oversight. Thune said he has been working with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) to reintroduce the bill "hopefully soon." House GOP…

33e1d7779a:f194f3824ccf7c41.title: Trump's $5,000 checks get chilly Senate GOP reception
33e1d7779a:f194f3824ccf7c41.author: Erin Davis
33e1d7779a:f194f3824ccf7c41.summary: Data: OMB ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals Senate Republicans are doubtful — and, in some cases, dismissive — of President Trump's proposal to give Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans keep control of Congress. Why it matters: Trump's proposal isn't dead on arrival. But Republicans aren't exactly lining up behind it either. "I am withholding judgment on the bill until I see their list of pay-fors," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said. "I don't support going and borrowing $1.2 trillion to be able to write the checks." "I would need to see details on it," Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) said. Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) said he wasn't sure about the mechanics of the proposal but that he's "also worrying about $40 trillion in debt." "You know, there's no specific proposal out there," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said. "And obviously, however that were to come together, Congress would have a big role in determining." Zoom in: There are two massive unknowns about the " Trump Dividend " that the president promised in Dallas last week: eligibility and price tag. Vice President Vance has suggested that wealthy Americans wouldn't receive the payment. If every "every adult citizen in the United States" were eligible, as Trump suggested, it could cost some $1.3 trillion. That would be more than three times what the U.S. collects annually from tariffs and other customs duties and fees. The intrigue: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who frequently defers to Trump, said Sunday that Congress would have to approve the payments. Asked in NBC's "Meet the Press" if he'd commit that the checks will be sent, Johnson said, "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else." Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) told Axios: "Well, if it happens, I'm recommending to people that they put it away in order to pay for the additional inflation. We will see." — Axios' Kate Santaliz contributed reporting for this story.

33e1d7779a:4e8be7ac90621d77.title: McConnell returns to Capitol after 3-month absence

Why it matters: The Kentucky Republican's return could finally unjam the farm bill — and put some MAGA world rumors to rest about his ability to do the job. McConnell arrived in a wheelchair and spoke briefly to reporters, joking that after years of avoiding their questions, he "wasn't sure how many of you would be here today. But I'm glad to see you. It's time to get back to work." He did not take questions but cast a vote Monday evening in favor of Matthew Byrne's nomination to be a district judge in Ohio. ' McConnell said he was ready to work on the farm bill, as well as on supporting NATO and Ukraine. Driving the news: " Today, I'll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June," McConnell said in a Monday evening statement. "I'm really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues." He described his recovery as "a long and often frustrating process," noting "the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier." McConnell added, "I'm still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me." What to watch: Whether the Senate Agriculture Committee will set a hearing this week to finally move the farm bill forward with McConnell's help. Catch up quick: McConnell, 84, was last seen at the Capitol on June 11. Since then, his team has provided few details about his health, fueling rampant online speculation. McConnell said in July that he fell at his home in June, briefly lost consciousness and was treated for mild pneumonia after he was hospitalized. The last official update came Aug. 6, when McConnell's office announced that he had been discharged from a rehabilitation facility and would continue recovering at home. Kentucky Gov.…

33e1d7779a:16ad119b8cbd3782.title: Trump DHS whistleblower alleges workers lied to access state voter data
33e1d7779a:16ad119b8cbd3782.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:16ad119b8cbd3782.summary: Department of Homeland Security employees were instructed to access state voter databases in ways a whistleblower alleges violate state law, according to a new report. Why it matters: The policy signals the Trump administration's persistence in trying to root out purported voter fraud by any means necessary. Driving the news: The whistleblower report , released by Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), details a protected whistleblower disclosure that "reveals serious allegations of illegal and inappropriate activities" within DHS' Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate. Employees have been asked to access sensitive voter information in state voter databases of people flagged by DHS as potential "unlawful voters," the report says. The whistleblower says the process can result in errors involving naturalized U.S. citizens, potentially subjecting them to secondary customs screenings at airports, or criminal referrals to Homeland Security Investigations. Zoom in: Some states, such as Virginia and Florida, require users signing onto the databases to legally confirm that they are the voter or an expressly authorized representative, meaning federal officers are effectively making false statements to access private records, the report says. Officers are also under tremendous pressure to review and verify a person's citizenship status in 12 minutes and enter it into a law enforcement record. The whistleblower says officers were told to rely on data they knew could be inaccurate, and employees' training on the new procedures amounted to a less-than-two-hour video. As a result, U.S. citizens are being investigated through the initiative "without their knowledge or ability to correct erroneous data," the report says. When officers questioned the practice, they were told individual officers would not be held personally liable for the searches, which the report says could indicate that the agency "is aware that the activity may be illegal."…

"The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax," he said, referring to the recent wave of warnings about catastrophic AI risks. Huang told Trump: "We're going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people." Zoom out: Huang separately addressed the AI safety fears that erupted over the weekend, striking a more nuanced tone than Trump. He said warnings from whistleblowers should be taken seriously, praising Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon for having "great courage" to raise his concerns about the company's AI development going too quickly. Yes, but: Huang rejected predictions that AI could end the world as "not grounded in science." He said AI companies should pause or pace their work "if they feel that their company is out of control." The big picture: Huang has repeatedly dismissed AI doomer fears , suggesting that some cybersecurity alarm around AI can help drum up business for the security industry.
